News.title: Protesters swarm Portsmouth hotel after 'mistaking Pakistan cricket team for migrants'
News.content:
Protesters swarm Portsmouth hotel after 'mistaking Pakistan cricket team for migrants'

Around 40 to 50 protesters swarmed the Marriott Hotel in Portsmouth on Tuesday evening in an apparent case of mistaken identity

View 2 Images Protesters swarmed outside the Marriott Hotel in Portsmouth

A crowd of protesters gathered outside a four-star hotel under the mistaken belief that asylum seekers were being put up there, when in fact the venue was hosting a Pakistani cricket team.

‌



A Reform UK councillor revealed that around 40 to 50 people descended on the Marriott Hotel in Portsmouth – where rooms regularly cost upwards of £120 a night – on Tuesday evening, just a day after demonstrators had attempted to block migrants from being transported for processing in the Eastney area of the city.

‌



Hampshire County Council Reform UK councillor George Madgwick said on social media that local residents had asked him to attend the hotel before he agreed to meet with the management. The protesters had wrongly mistaken the Pakistan under-19 national cricket team for migrants, he said.

‌



He said: "I visited the manager and the hotel explained it was a Pakistani Cricket team staying. The cricket team coach came to speak to me personally and I saw proof (hotel were happy to provide)."

The North East Havant councillor went on to explain that he then addressed the gathered crowd outside to set the record straight, and they "immediately (the crowd) respectfully accepted that" and dispersed within five minutes.

‌



He said in the post: "There were reports that possible migrants were staying in the Marriott hotel. I can confirm that is NOT the case. Please don't attend the hotel."

View 2 Images Protesters clashed with riot police when migrants landed at Eastney (Image: Jamie Lashmar/PA Wire)

The councillor maintained that the Government must understand why such events take place, saying: "If the government don't get a grip on this boat crisis we will see this more and more." He claimed the protesters were not "bad people" but instead people who feel strongly about their neighbourhood.

Article continues below

However, Stand up to Racism Portsmouth also wrote: "Yesterday (Tuesday 8th) some non-white people were spotted amongst the guests at a Marriott Hotel in Portsmouth. Anywhere else in the world, it would just be a case of business-as-usual.

"Allowing racists to mobilise like this every time they become suspicious of any group of non-white people in Portsmouth is extremely dangerous. It is racism in action and it has to stop."

News.title: Heathrow and Gatwick - live: More than 300 flights cancelled today after air traffic control glitch
News.content:
EasyJet, BA, Ryanair, KLM and Eurowings flights have all been cancelled at major airports including Heathrow and Gatwick today following the air traffic control issues on Tuesday

Flights are still being cancelled and delayed across the UK - after an air traffic control "technical issue" on Tuesday - as a Government minister said she did not believe the chaos was "unavoidable".

When asked whether Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander and Prime Minister still have confidence in NATS (National Air Traffic Services) CEO Martin Rolfe, a spokesperson said: "We have confidence in him and he's been tasked with an investigation."

But Ms Alexander told the House of Commons "I do not believe this issue was unavoidable".

More than 300 flights have been cancelled today - including at Heathrow and Gatwick - on top of 1,300 flights from UK airports axed on Tuesday, according to Flightradar24. Tens of thousands of holidaymakers have been left stranded for hours, with distressed passengers reporting being left waiting on runways.

A NATS spokesperson apologised for the delays and advised passengers to check with their airline before travelling to airports.

Mr Rolfe has apologised, telling the BBC that there would be a full investigation into what had gone wrong. Asked about the cause of the problem, Mr Rolfe said a "thorough" investigation would be carried out, but ruled out a cyber-attack.

News.title: 'Harry and Meghan risk history repeating dark period for Royals amid tensions with the Firm'
News.content:
'Harry and Meghan risk history repeating dark period for Royals amid tensions with the Firm'

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have barely been in the country two weeks - creating more questions than answers as to why they here and what their intensions are

View 3 Images Tensions within the Royals after Harry and Meghan's return to the UK risk repeating a dark period of the monarchy's history (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Leaks, counter leaks and dueling media campaigns between two camps unable to work together. An intense rivalry galvanised by warring courts, unable to pull back from the brink of internal destruction.

‌



Indeed, the War of the Waleses - involving Prince Charles and Princess Diana during the most brutal separation during the 90s - will forever be remembered as one of the most challenging periods for the royal family. And yet, more than 30 years on, history appears to be in danger of repeating itself.

‌



Just two weeks from touching down on British soil - six years after leaving it all behind on the crassly coined ‘Freedom Flight’ - Harry and Meghan have returned to the UK.

‌



View 3 Images Prince Charles and Princess Diana engaged in a brutal briefing war against each other when their marriage broke down (Image: Getty Images)

Should Prince Harry and Meghan Markle stop using their royal titles in public? Take our poll and have your say READ MORE :

Depending on what news outlet you have consumed this week, the sequel that absolutely no one had asked for, will last between six months and 15 years. Best buckle up then!

‌



Apart from the fact, no one quite knows what they are doing here. True enough, Harry may have been homesick. He may have even yearned for the British autumn after what must be an intolerable time in almost constant sunshine on the Californian coast.

Who could really blame him for choosing a quaint British school in the countryside for his children? And maybe, as far fetched as it may sound, Meghan has actually got a job offer with a Netflix smasher.

Yet, none of this has stopped the rumour mill in suggesting the money is running out and they’ve been forced to come back to the drawing board and have another crack at making things work with the family they’ve spent the last six years running roughshod over. The thing is, no one actually knows. It wouldn’t be that surprising even if Harry and Meghan didn’t!

‌



View 3 Images Harry and Meghan have returned to Britain for an "extended stay" according to their team (Image: PA)

The Sussexes' return to Britain has brought more questions than answers. Top of the tree is undoubtedly what do they actually want? Do they, or Harry at least, really want complete reconciliation? Would he even know how to go about it? Developments over the last few weeks would suggest not.

‌



Waiting until three days before global news breaks of your return before telling your dad - the actual King - of your homecoming, might not be considered putting one’s best foot forward. And then we get to the startling coincidences of times gone by.

Barely a fortnight has passed and the briefing wars have begun. The pattern was already so heavily stitched into the fabric of this story, of course, dating back to February 2020.

The terms of their exit was determined by the royal family - only for Harry and Meghan to publish a lengthy statement “clarifying” what the palace had put out just hours earlier. In more recent years there has been a cascade of leaking to journalists on their ‘friendly’ list detailing, to varying levels of dismay, everything from how their children Archie and Lilibet were not invited to the Coronation, to the King no t answering Harry's calls.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

While uncertainty continues to linger in the air, this week the King, through the Lord Chamberlain, got on the front foot by extinguishing any hope the Sussexes may have of coming back to the royal fold. His message, in a letter to local authorities and basically anyone else looking to engage with them, could not have been clearer. They aren't coming back and they don't represent The Firm.

Without drawing breath, Team Sussex draws on the tried and trusted methods of outrage of the past. The letter goes public, the Sussexes relay their dismay, they were “surprised” at the lack of respect. I’ll leave that with you to consider for just a moment.

Article continues below

Get the inside scoop on the monarchy with Mirror Royal WHATSAPP GROUP: Be first to get the biggest royal bombshells and exclusives to your phone by joining our Royal WhatsApp here. We also treat our community members to special offers, promotions, and adverts from us and our partners. If you don’t like our community, you can check out any time you like. If you’re curious, you can read our Privacy Notice. NEWSLETTER: Or sign up to the Mirror's Royal newsletter here to get all the biggest royal news and exclusive pictures, straight to your inbox.

Claim and counter claim reach the public sphere. Harry hasn’t had the decency to call his father - “oh no he has!” the other side cries. Round and round we go.

So where does this leave us, or rather, them? It’s hard to believe it has only been a few weeks since the once considered impossible scenario of repatriation filtered through and then became a reality. It’s going to be a slog to the end of the year if this is a sign of things to come.

News.title: Lack of medication contributed to Sir Richard Branson's wife's tragic death, inquest finds
News.content:
Lack of medication contributed to Sir Richard Branson's wife's tragic death, inquest finds

Lady Joan Sarah Drummond Branson died aged 80 in November last year at The Lister Hospital from a blood clot

View 4 Images (Image: Chris Pizzello/Invision/AP)

New details have emerged regarding the death of Sir Richard Branson's wife.

‌



Lady Joan Sarah Drummond Branson died aged 80 in November last year at The Lister Hospital from a blood clot on November 24 last year at The Lister Hospital from complications following a fall-induced back injury two weeks earlier.

‌



A private hospital’s failure to provide preventative medication contributed to the death of Sir Richard Branson’s wife, an inquest has concluded. She suffered a cardiac arrest at the private Lister Hospital in Chelsea, west London, which is owned and operated by HCA Healthcare.

‌



Westminster Coroner’s Court heard on Wednesday that she died after suffering a pulmonary embolism, a sudden, dangerous blockage in a lung artery, resulting from deep vein thrombosis.

The virtual inquest heard that Lady Joan was admitted to the hospital on November 17 after a fall weeks earlier on Necker Island – a private luxury retreat in the Caribbean’s British Virgin Islands owned by her billionaire husband.

View 4 Images (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Professor Fiona Wilcox, senior coroner for Inner West London, said Lady Joan did not receive prophylactic anticoagulants at the hospital despite a “very high risk of developing deep vein thrombosis”.

Giving her conclusion, the coroner said: “I do find her death would have likely been prevented and the lack of anticoagulation did cause or contribute to her death probably.”

Lady Joan also did not receive an immediate Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) assessment to check her risk of developing harmful blood clots, the inquest heard. Dr Adams said “any patient who comes into hospital should have an immediate VTE assessment to determine their risk of bleeding”.

‌



Lady Joan’s daughter, Dr Holly Branson, told the inquest that her mother also did not have Thrombo-Embolus Deterrent stockings – which are designed to prevent deep vein thrombosis by promoting blood flow in the lower legs – for the first 48 hours after being admitted.

The hospital’s admitting doctor, Dr Basir Kunduzi, did not complete a bleeding risk assessment on the day of her admission, the inquest heard. Dr Kunduzi said Lady Joan “should have been on anti-coagulants” and her death led him to “reflect on my role as a doctor” and the importance of “good communication between team members”.

Resident medical officer Dr Nevil Pavithran told the inquest that Lady Joan “should have received her first dose of anticoagulation prophylaxis within 12 hours of admission”, adding this not occurring caused a “significant risk”. The doctor said he had “spent quite a lot of time going over the incidents” and said he felt he “should have been more forceful”.

‌



View 4 Images (Image: Getty Images)

Lady Joan’s consultant, Dr Inaki Bovil, said there had been a “lot of work at the Lister to make it more robust around VTE and risk prevention” and to “prevent this from happening again”.

Earlier this year, Sir Richard and Joan's daughter Holly, 44, said that the family was not looking to blame anyone for her death.

‌



However, the inquest has looked at whether Lady Branson should have been prescribed blood thinners and if she was wearing anti-clot stockings at the time of her death. Speaking at the hearing at Inner West London Coroners’ Court, Holly said: “I believe mum had great care. The doctors saved her life three years ago, giving us all three more years together. We just want to help other families if there are any lessons to be learned.”

Senior Coroner Professor Fiona Wilcox previously told the court the inquest would establish whether or not Lady Branson was wearing Thrombo-Embolus Deterrent - or TED - stockings, which reduce the risk of blood clots and are worn by patients during periods of inactivity.

Prof Wilcox told the court that statements from an expert witness would be needed to determine whether a prescription of the anti-coagulant Heparin “would have prevented Lady Branson’s death”, given that she had a previous history of clots.

‌



An expert haematologist will present a report of their findings at the inquest, scheduled for September. Joan’s history of blood clots went back to at least 2010. In 2018, Sir Richard shared that one morning around eight years previously Joan had woken up to find her leg three times its normal size - which led to her undergoing a novel new treatment.

She had suffered a series of clots from her ankle up to her groin - the “worst case” doctors at that hospital had ever seen. Sir Richard said: “She was in great danger of a pulmonary embolism, as bits of the clot threatened to break away and travel to her lungs. The doctors put her on a drug called Warfarin, pulled a compression stocking over her leg and told her that over a number of years the leg would gradually improve, but that at any stage she might suffer a major pulmonary embolism that could kill her.”

View 4 Images (Image: PA)

‌



But she underwent surgery that put a tiny umbrella inside her leg so that if any clot did break off, it could not enter her lungs. “Two days later, she nearly skipped out of the building!” he added.

He broke the news of his wife’s passing on Instagram on November 25 last year. He said: “Heartbroken to share that Joan, my wife and partner for 50 years, has passed away. She was the most wonderful mum and grandmum our kids and grandkids could have ever wished for. She was my best friend, my rock, my guiding light, my world. Love you forever, Joan x”

A day later, on virgin.com, he wrote a longer tribute. He said: “Joan was the most wonderful partner, friend, mum and grandmother we could ever have wished for. Holly, Sam and I are all together now, doing our best to smile through the tears and to focus on all the good things she brought into our world. There are so many.

‌



“We had a lovely lunch that day. She was in positive spirits and getting stronger. She smiled at me, that radiant smile that lit up her whole face, the same smile I fell in love with the very first moment I saw her, half a century ago. Then suddenly, she was gone, quickly and painlessly. And thankfully, I was right by her side. It brings us all great comfort to know we were together.”

Sir Richard and Joan’s love story began in 1976, when the fledgling tycoon met the then Joan Templeman at The Manor, the live-in recording studio he had built for Virgin Records. She worked in an antiques shop called Dodo in Notting Hill, close to the Virgin office.

Glasgow-born Joan was a former model, at the heart of Swinging London’s vibrant music and fashion scene. Sir Richard found excuses to visit her shop, amassing a huge collection of antiques he didn’t really need.

Article continues below

At the time, Joan was still married to her first husband, rock pianist Ronnie Leahy, and the pair embarked on an affair. Joan took a while to warm to the charm offensive, but Sir Richard’s persistence - lavish gifts, impromptu trips, even halting a taxiing plane at Heathrow to whisk her aboard - wore down her reservations.

Tragedy struck when Sir Richard and Joan’s first child, Clare Sarah, was still-born in 1979. Joan would go on to support premature birth-charities as part of her philanthropic work later in life. The couple’s children Holly and Sam were born in 1981 and 1985. Joan’s five grandchildren also survive her.

News.title: Heathrow chaos as weddings put at risk and disruption set to last all week after NATS meltdown
News.content:
Heathrow chaos as weddings put at risk and disruption set to last all week after NATS meltdown

Tens of thousands of passengers have been caught up in the chaos at airports across the UK as the knock-on effects from the NATS air control failure continue to be felt

View 5 Images Tired passengers at Heathrow took to sleeping on airport trays (Image: Daily Mirror)

Furious passengers at Heathrow have told of their ‘24 hours from hell’ as flight chaos rumbled on at Britain’s busiest airport.

‌



Nearly 300 flights were cancelled across the UK and many more delayed on Wednesday, while experts warned the knock-on effects from the catastrophic failure of the NATS air control system would continue to be felt for the rest of the week.

‌



Aviation analytics company Cirium said 291 flights had been cancelled, around 5% of the 5,869 scheduled and over twice the amount expected on a normal day. At Heathrow, the Mirror saw passengers grow increasingly exasperated as airline staff did their best while delivering more bad news.

‌



View 5 Images Disruption from the NATS air control failure is set to last all week (Image: Daily Mirror)

NATS air traffic control boss Martin Rolfe urged to quit by Ryanair and WizzAir chiefs after three airport meltdowns READ MORE :

Heathrow and Gatwick live: Nearly 300 flights cancelled today after air traffic chaos READ MORE :

Some stranded passengers took to resting on blankets, baggage trays and trolleys after being told they would not be able to get on a plane until tomorrow. Issues with luggage proved a particular sticking point as people crowded around uniformed airline workers to demand answers over where their bags were.

One family told us they were due to be at a wedding in Lisbon in 24 hours' time, and were supposed to have arrived with British Airways the night before. Instead, Patrick Onu, 36, his wife Crystal and their two young children spent Wednesday morning desperately trying to pick up their luggage from Heathrow, which contained their wedding outfits.

‌



View 5 Images Patrick Onu, 36, needs to get his young children and wife Crystal to Portugal for a wedding (Image: Daily Mirror)

They were due to catch a replacement flight from Birmingham at 5pm.

Patrick said: "My wife is part of the bridal team. Last night we were actually ushered out of the airport through the tannoy system - everyone had to leave ‘cause there's too many people, so no one could wait for their suitcases.

‌



"We were asked to come back in the morning, and we still can't get our suitcases. We've been on the phone to the airline since 4am this morning, and we’ve got a connecting flight from Birmingham tonight.

"So now I have to drive to Birmingham to get a connecting flight to Amsterdam, then to Lisbon, with two kids. And I can't even go there with our suitcases, or even their nappies."

View 5 Images Alice Haynes (right), sister Chloe (centre) and grandma Brenda had been ready to set off (Image: Daily Mirror)

‌



Sisters Chloe and Alice Haynes, both in their 20s, were planning to travel to Toronto with their grandma Brenda, 80, to see a close family friend. They had seen their two-week family holiday cut down to 12 days after their direct flight was cancelled.

All three have now been forced to rebook onto a connecting American Airlines flight via Philadelphia, and leave their suitcases at Heathrow.

Alice said: "My grandma hasn't been on a plane in like 20 years. And it's all gone wrong. So now she doesn't want to go on a plane again!" Chloe added: "The communication here has been rubbish."

‌



A spokesperson for British Airways said: "We're doing everything we can to get them to where they need to be and ask them to remain patient while we work to find solutions for everyone."

A bride-to-be and her 77-year-old father were also stranded in Heathrow Airport as they tried out how to figure out how to get to her wedding in Italy. After their early Wednesday morning flight was cancelled, they now hope to travel to Gatwick, fly to Milan, catch another flight to Naples early on Thursday, and then a boat to Ischia.

The wedding is on Sunday, but events start on Friday with a welcome to their friends, who have already arrived.

‌



The father-of-the bride, who flew from Thailand via the UK for the ceremony, said: "We've been delayed and unfortunately my daughter's been emotionally disturbed because she's been organising this for the last two years."

Bosses at the under-fire NATS air control firm said they had ruled out a cyber attack as the cause of the major outage.

CEO Martin Rolfe said: "We will be doing a very, very thorough and full investigation. We have at this point ruled out cyber. We don't believe it was a cyber attack."

‌



View 5 Images It is the third major air control failure in just over three years (Image: Daily Mirror)

Asked about the severe disruption at airports across the country, the Prime Minister's official spokesman told reporters: "You've seen this morning that the Transport Secretary met the chief of NATS to raise significant concerns at the scale of disruption on behalf of both passengers and industry.

"She's asked him to carry out a full investigation into what happened to make sure that lessons are learned, so that this doesn't happen again. She set a deadline for them to report back in a week's time.

Article continues below

"And through our Civil Aviation Bill, which returns to Parliament today, we will make sure air passengers get stronger protection of rights around cancellations, delays, and passenger support."

News.title: Explosives alert closes Swiss-German border crossing as bomb squad rushes to scene
News.content:
Explosives alert closes Swiss-German border crossing as bomb squad rushes to scene

Police and a bomb squad have swarmed a Swiss-German border crossing after a dog alerted customs officers to explosives inside a German vehicle

View 2 Images Police are at the scene (stock) (Image: Getty Images)

Police have closed down a Swiss-German border crossing after explosives were detected during a routine inspection of a car.

‌



Sniffer dogs alerted Swiss customs officers to a German vehicle at the Rheinfelden border crossing at around 1pm local time, Bild reports.

‌



The German Federal Police swarmed the scene with a bomb disposal team as two busy highways were closed.

‌



The suspect's vehicle was stopped as it entered Switzerland from Germany after authorities noticed that the registered owner was suspected of a crime.

View 2 Images The car was stopped at the Swiss-German border in Rheinfelden (file image) (Image: U. Baumgarten via Getty Images)

‌



The Baden-Württemberg state police reported the vehicle before it was searched by explosive detection dogs.

On two occasions, the dogs alerted officers to the car, indicating the presence of explosives.

The A861 in Germany and the A3 in Switzerland have been closed in both directions while authorities continue investigating the scene. Disruption is expected to last into the evening.

Article continues below

The Rheinfelden border crossing connects Germany to Rheinfelden in Switzerland across the Rhine River. Around 28,000 vehicles pass through the highway every day.

News.title: PMQs RECAP: Andy Burnham suggests he won't slash benefits to fund extra defence spending in Kemi Badenoch clash
News.content:
Andy Burnham has said funding national security 'can’t come at the expense of social security' at his second appearance at Prime Minister’s Questions

PMQs: Andy Burnham says Badenoch 'has to do better than that'

Andy Burnham has said funding national security "can’t come at the expense of social security" at his second appearance at Prime Minister’s Questions.

The PM - who has already said welfare spending needs cutting - clashed with Tory leader Kemi Badenoch over Tory plans to slash welfare spending to fund defence. He told the Commons Labour MPs "will not be forced to choose between the two", as he criticised the Conservatives’ plan to cut housing benefit to fund defence.

During the session, the PM also addressed the UK’s decision to slap sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank The UK was among 12 countries backing the move, which has sparked fury in Israel.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband rejected criticism from Britain's chief rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis, who branded it a "truly dark day for British Jews" and said the measure would embolden those who stir up hatred. Mr Miliband said announcing the measures in response to settler violence in the West Bank was "the right thing to do".

Mr Burnham tells the Commons his government will always stand with the "underdog", adding: "Leadership is about taking action where there is injustice, where we need to correct unfairness."

News.title: Should Prince Harry and Meghan Markle stop using their royal titles in public? Take our poll and have your say
News.content:
Should Prince Harry and Meghan Markle stop using their royal titles in public? Take our poll and have your say

This week has been tense in the Royal family, with a main focus on Meghan and Harr, as a shock announcement from the King was handed out to a number of people explaining the couple should be treated as private citizens

View 2 Images The Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped down from their royal commitments years ago (Image: PA)

Just two weeks after the Duke and Duchess returned to the UK, a fresh row has erupted over how the couple should be referred to.

‌



While the public are conflicted on how best to address the couple, the King has now made his position clear, with guidance issued on his behalf stating that Harry and Meghan should not use their HRH styles, which remain in abeyance, and that they “do not represent the sovereign” while making public appearances. The guidance is understood to have been sent to government figures, the military and lord lieutenants, also confirmed the couple should be treated as “private citizens”.

‌



Harry and Meghan stepped back from carrying out duties on behalf of the Sovereign in 2020, meaning they were no longer working members of the Royal Family, before moving to the United States. But the latest move appears to have caught Team Sussex off guard.

‌



View 2 Images There is a debate over whether Harry and Meghan should continue their royal duties (Image: PA ROTA / PA ROTA - B68 / Avalon)

Prince George wears Eton uniform after arriving at £63k-a-year school with proud William and Kate READ MORE :

The Sussexes’ team was given the guidance shortly before it was made public and later said it had not had enough time to clarify points before its release. The row has since reignited debate over whether Harry and Meghan should continue to use their royal titles.

‌



On Tuesday morning, ITV presenter Cat Deeley said the couple were a “huge asset” to the Royal Family because of their global reach. Ashley James said it was ‘a shame’ the situation could not be dealt with privately, adding that Harry remained a royal, officially or unofficially, and that the monarchy would be “so much stronger” with Harry and Meghan.

The Sussexes are also understood to have taken issue with being described as “private citizens”. The Telegraph reports: “The duke is understood to have taken particular issue with the notion that the couple were to be treated as private citizens. If that were the case, it was claimed, such formal guidance would not be required.

Article continues below

“The Sussexes prefer the term ‘public figures’, and would have liked an acknowledgement that, on a personal level, they remained members of the Royal Family, despite no longer receiving public funding.”

The debate comes as Meghan has not been seen publicly since the family returned to Britain and may remain out of the spotlight for several weeks while helping Archie and Lilibet settle into their new life.

Harry, meanwhile, is expected to take a more visible role and increase his charity work in the UK, with the Duke due to attend the WellChild Awards later this month.

News.title: Police launch criminal investigation into Reform UK donations
News.content:
In the news report, an undercover investigator posing as the son of an American donor is recorded raising a concern that his father wouldn't be able to directly donate to the party within the law.

Electoral law states that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.

Jukes appears to suggest that the donation could be in the UK-based son's name, although the money would have come from his American father.

Elsewhere, James Orr, the party's head of policy suggests that the father could pay for opinion polling to support one of Reform's campaigns.

Farage and Jukes were also filmed at a lunch in Clacton where it is suggested the US donor, who was being played by an actor, gives Â£500,000 to Reform through his son.

Farage told the BBC he "frankly wasn't listening" to the discussion about the potential donation. Channel 4 News has said the payment was never made.

He dismissed the comments made by his aide in the film as "loose pub talk including a couple of boasts that simply were not true".

Jukes has denied "any wrongdoing" and said he had "stepped back from politics in order to clear my name".

Last week, Orr told Sky News he would cooperate with the party's internal investigation "fully".

The Met had already been investigating whether payments to Reform in the weeks before the last election complied with donation laws.

The probe is examining donations given directly to the party by Fiona Cottrell, mother of longstanding Nigel Farage ally, George Cottrell.

It is also examining payments from a company controlled by Reform's deputy leader Richard Tice, which received Â£1m from Fiona Cottrell in June 2024.

A Verbatim Investigations spokesperson said: "Verbatim will cooperate with the police's investigation."

Labour Party Chair Bridget Phillipson said: "Farage needs to wake up and realise the buck stops with him.

"Reform's failure to take responsibility for their actions shows just how unfit they are for office."

The Liberal Democrat's Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart said: "Every Reform MP urgently needs to state whether they or their campaigns have benefited from any foreign money."

Zack Polanski, leader of the Green Party in England and Wales, said: "Nigel Farage and Lee Anderson hoped they could pin all this on two of their most senior advisors, but they have more questions to answer about how much they knew."

News.title: National security can't come at expense of social security, Burnham says
News.content:
In the Commons session, Burnham repeated that the government would meet the Nato target of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, with a target date for hitting the 3% figure set out in the spending review in the spring.

The PM said he had appointed John Healey, who resigned as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary over the government's failure to commit to a 3% increase by 2030, "because of his strong commitment to the defence of this nation".

However, Badenoch hit back that 2035 was "a decade away" and "the threats are now".

She questioned whether Burnham was "unable" or "just unwilling" to meet the 2030 target.

In response, Burnham insisted: "This chancellor of all chancellors will be willing to provide that funding to our armed forces."

However, he rejected a Conservative plan to partly fund increased defence spending by saving at least Â£4bn through reforms to housing benefit.

"I don't think, myself, that taking Â£4bn out of housing benefit is going to get the right consensus around this issue because that would create levels of homelessness in this country... that we wouldn't have seen before, hundreds of thousands of children in temporary accommodation," he said.

"Yes, we do everything to support our national security, but it can't come at the expense of social security."

He added: "This side of the House will not be forced to choose between the two and we will set out a plan to get to 3.5% by 2035 at the spending review."

Badenoch said Burnham's comments were "unbelievable", adding: "We need to fund our defence, not spend all of our money on welfare."

Burnham insisted he would "bring the welfare budget down" by tackling the number of young people not in education, employment or training.

"That's the Labour way to get the welfare bill down," he said.

"That is the right way to fund defence."

Badenoch accused Burnham of being "continuity Keir".

"He's pretending that he's the change candidate. But the fact is, he's still failing to cut welfare," she said.

As prime minister, Sir Keir attempted to cut disability benefits but was forced to row back on the plans in the face of opposition from Labour MPs.

Cutting the welfare bill is a key part of Tory proposals for funding increased defence spending.

Spending on benefits has ballooned in recent years and is forecast to rise to Â£408.6bn in 2030/31, according to figures from the Department for Work and Pensions.

There is particular concern about the nearly one million young people in the UK who are not in education, employment or training â known as "Neets".

The government has asked former minister Alan Milburn to look into the issue and he is expected to publish his final recommendations for how to tackle the problem shortly.

News.title: Watch: Europe's royalty pay last respects to King Harald V in Norway
News.content:
Tributes have been paid to King Harald V after his funeral in Norway's capital Oslo, with the Prince of Wales and other European royals among attendees.

Flags were raised from half-mast to mark the conclusion of a private ceremony at Akershus Fortress, where the king was laid to rest in the crypt of the Palace Chapel after a public service at Oslo Cathedral.

Tens of thousands of people lined the streets to pay their respects after 13 days of national mourning.

The new king Haakon VIII - Harald's son - and his family stood on the balcony of the Royal Palace and waved to thousands of people gathered outside.

The late monarch died in August after 35 years on the throne.

News.title: Miliband rejects chief rabbi's claim British Jews in greater danger after sanctions move
News.content:
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has rejected the chief rabbi's warning that British Jews are at greater risk after the UK announced sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Miliband said that as a "proud British Jew" he disagreed with UK Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis, who described the move as a "truly dark day" that would "succeed only in bolstering the very extremism they seek to target".

"We all need to do more to tackle antisemitism," Miliband said, "but I believe we can do that and stand up for British values".

The sanctions on trade with illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank come against a backdrop of rising antisemitic incidents across the UK.

The Community Security Trust (CST), an organisation that provides security support to the Jewish community, recorded 1,926 incidents of anti-Jewish hate across the UK in the first six months of 2026, a 21% increase on the same period in 2025.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham defended his government's decision, telling MPs that "Britain has to stand for fairness against injustice".

"Where people are being bullied out of their homes... we will always stand with the underdog," he said.

The Palestinian presidency welcomed the UK's decision, saying it was "an important step towards confronting Israel's colonial system and its violations against the Palestinian people".

There has been mixed reaction within the UK Jewish community on the sanctions and possible implications for security.

The chief rabbi called the government's announcement "little more than political flag bearing for mendacious anti-Israel rhetoric".

Sir Ephraim said: "Gesture politics of this kind feeds into an increasingly hostile discourse about Israel, and the cumulative effect of such punitive policies is to further embolden those, at home and abroad, who use hatred as a weapon against Jews."

Asked about Mirvis's comments, Miliband said: "I don't agree with the chief rabbi, somebody... of whom I have great respect."

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that "anyone who holds British Jews - or indeed Jews around the world - responsible for the actions of the Israeli government, is engaging in antisemitism, pure and simple".

Meanwhile, the Jewish Leadership Council (JLC) warned the government's decision "risks becoming a de facto boycott of Israel" and accused Miliband of "yielding to pressure from the most extreme elements of British society".

The Board of Deputies of British Jews said the decision to make the announcement before Rosh Hashanah - the Jewish New Year festival which begins on Friday - brings "concerns for communal security at their highest levels... felt particularly acutely by British Jews".

It added that the deteriorating relationship between the UK and Israel has the potential to "further inflame community tensions here too", while also noting it had warned the Israeli government over the "intolerable settler violence" that harms Israel's reputation.

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) announced on Wednesday that extra resources would be allocated during the Jewish High Holy Days to provide "extra visibility and security" and "ensure everyone can celebrate this time safely".

Ch Supt Dave Meeney said: "Our officers will continue working with Jewish communities as we head into this important period for their faith, which we understand is a time which may bring heightened concern for the community."

News.title: 'We were raped and exploited by a drug gang as teenagers', women tell BBC of their ordeal
News.content:
Warning: Contains details of sexual exploitation

Christine is one of four women who have chosen to waive their anonymity and speak publicly to the BBC documentary, Britain's Forgotten Girls, about how they were targeted by criminals when they were children.

Their stories differ in detail, but reveal strikingly similar patterns of abuse.

All four describe being targeted by boys and older men connected to drugs gangs, manipulated into abusive relationships, then repeatedly sexually exploited.

All believe the authorities failed to protect them and did not take their allegations seriously.

The sexual and criminal exploitation of girls by drug gangs has long been overshadowed in public discussion by the focus on sexual grooming gangs, according to front-line social workers and experts in the field.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

News.title: Hundreds mourn police officer killed in wrong-way A66 crash
News.content:
Hundreds have turned out for the funeral of one of the police officers killed in a wrong-way crash.

PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, died when a Volkswagen Passat collided with their marked armed response car on the A66 at South Bank, near Middlesbrough, on 22 August. Five young men were also killed.

A full ceremonial police funeral took place for PC Blades in Hartlepool earlier, with hundreds of officers from Cleveland and forces across the country lining the street in a guard of honour.

Speaking on behalf of his family, Cleveland Police Federation chair Lauren Somerville said "life feels unbearably quiet" without the father-of-two's "silly jokes" and laughter.

Members of other emergency services were present at St Joseph's Roman Catholic Church, alongside community leaders and politicians.

Cleveland Police chief constable Victoria Fuller greeted mourners at the entrance to the church.

Policing minister Sarah Jones and Home Office minister Anna Turley also attended.

News.title: Mother demands answers, weeks after black woman found hanging from Mississippi tree
News.content:
Spivey last saw her daughter alive on 26 July, when Fortune had travelled from Mississippi, where she had lived for roughly the last decade, to Kentucky, where Spivey lives, for a family reunion.

The next time she saw her daughter - in a funeral home, days before her burial - she could barely look at her body.

"I didn't look straight at her. Her daddy did," she said. "I kind of looked from the side."

Spivey remembered their last conversation. "She was talking about, you know, maybe even coming home," she explained.

Fortune's death has left the community concerned that racial violence in Mississippi could be on the rise again. And in the absence of concrete details about the case, their suspicions are left to fester.

Fortune's death was the third incident in Mississippi in less than a year where police found someone dead and hanged from a tree.

The other two bodies - one black male, one white - were discovered in September 2025, on the exact same day.

Both were ruled a suicide, though the mother of one of the deceased - Trey Reed - contests those findings.

Fed-up residents have launched an online petition, which has gathered more than 50,000 signatures, for an independent investigation into the state's chief medical examiner, Dr Staci Turner, over the handling of a recent spate of cases involving people of colour. Another petition asks for the FBI to launch an investigation into Fortune's death

The BBC has asked Turner for comment.

Jackson City Councilman Kenneth Stokes has also expressed concerns about the police investigation, saying he'd been outside the home where Fortune was thought to have lived multiple times and has never seen officers.

"All cases are important, but this one - a hanging in Mississippi - should rise to the top of the food chain," Stokes said.

He told the BBC he sent letters to both federal prosecutors at the Mississippi US attorney's office and the FBI weeks ago, urging that the investigation was "in dire need of assistance". He has yet to hear back from either.

"Nothing from nobody," Stokes said. "It's like nobody cares."

The BBC has reached out to the Mississippi US attorney's office and the local FBI office for comment.

US Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett has similarly requested federal intervention. In a letter to the US Department of Justice, she asked for an investigation into recent deaths in Mississippi - including that of Tasia Fortune - calling them "possible cases of modern-day lynchings". She cited the state's "appalling historical reputation of violent terrorism against black Americans".

In addition to Mississippi, there have been multiple other cases nationally of black Americans found hanged from trees, including four in North Carolina this year alone. Three were ruled a suicide. An autopsy is pending for the fourth death.

The BBC has reached out to the justice department for comment.

Stokes is clear that he does not know whether Fortune's death was a lynching, or whether race played a part at all. Nor does he care. He just wants answers.

Brandon King, president of the student National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) chapter at nearby Jackson State University, said the mystery of Fortune's death, combined with minimal updates from police, has led him and others to be "extra cautious" around campus.

The feeling, King said, was that "hey, you could be next. This is in Jackson. This is in your backyard".

The thought is extra worrying, he continued, because "this is supposed to be the capital. This is where I'm supposed to feel the most safe".

As for Spivey, she cried before heading to a funeral home for her daughter, dreading having to fill out a death certificate and decide whether to cremate or bury her firstborn child.

She wanted to cremate her daughter but decided, in the end, for a burial. She said she was holding out hope there would be updates in the investigation, which might mean needing to exhume her corpse.

News.title: Man charged with assisting Russian intelligence service
News.content:
A 31-year-old British man has been charged under the National Security Act over alleged contact with Russia's military intelligence agency.

Joshua Cammidge, from Swindon, allegedly received instructions from an individual believed to be linked to the GRU Volunteer Corps, a group controlled by Russia's military intelligence agency, the Crown Prosecution service said.

He has been charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct.

He is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Thursday.

Cammidge was arrested at an address in Swindon on Friday by Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London officers, supported by officers from Wiltshire Police.

He was taken to a London police station and searches were carried out at a different address in Swindon, the Metropolitan Police said.

He was further arrested and detained under the National Security Act on Saturday.

News.title: Drug gangs exploited and raped us as teens, then police failed us, women tell BBC
News.content:
Warning: Contains details of sexual exploitation

"It was the thrill of being with a bad boy."

Christine was 13 when she began exchanging messages online with someone she believed was a teenage boy.

On their first meeting, she discovered he was a grown man 10 years older than herself. He also told her he was involved with gangs and drugs.

"I always knew, OK, he's probably hurt someone, but in terms of hurting me, I didn't think it would get to that point," she says.

Over the next few years, he would use Christine to courier drugs, subject her to extreme sexual exploitation, and assault her so violently she feared she might die.

Christine is one of four women who have chosen to waive their anonymity and speak publicly to the BBC documentary, Britain's Forgotten Girls, about how they were targeted by criminals when they were children.

Their stories, covering 2002 to last year, differ in detail - but reveal strikingly similar patterns of abuse. All four describe being targeted by boys and older men connected to drug gangs, manipulated into abusive relationships, then repeatedly sexually exploited.

All believe the authorities failed to protect them and did not take their allegations seriously.

The sexual and criminal exploitation of girls by drug gangs has long been overshadowed in public discussion by the focus on sexual grooming gangs, according to front-line social workers and experts in the field.

"For grooming gangs, the primary purpose is often the sexual exploitation of those girls, but the primary purpose of a drug gang is to make money off selling drugs and other criminal activity," says Connie Muttock from the children's charity, Centre for Young Lives.

Girls are brought in to generate money, says Muttock, but many are also sexually abused by gang members.

News.title: Learner drivers still forced to wait months to book tests
News.content:
Learner drivers have to wait an average 20 weeks, or around five months, before booking a practical test, according to new figures, despite attempts to reduce delays.

The data from the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) for August is only a marginal improvement from 20.2 weeks in July.

The average wait time between booking and sitting a test is unchanged at 11.1 weeks.

The DVSA initially had a target of reducing the average waiting time to seven weeks by the end of last year. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander pushed the target back to summer 2026, but subsequently admitted even that would not be possible.

The DVSA made a number of changes to its practical driving test booking system earlier this year.

Only the learner driver themself is now able to book their driving test, blocking an instructor or third parties from booking using the learner's details.

There is also a geographical restriction which means a learner can only book a test at their three local test centres, rather than one at the other side of the country if they found a test available.

The number of times a would-be driver can swap a test date has also been restricted.

News.title: Divorcing abusive husband cost woman £105k
News.content:
A woman who endured years of abusive controlling behaviour by her ex-husband says it has cost her more than Â£105,000 to divorce him.

Annabelle Boucher, 48, from Somerset, wants the law changed after she paid Â£75,000 to David Rogers, 61, despite him admitting to coercive and controlling behaviour. She also had to pay her legal costs.

"I thought being stuck in this relationship I couldn't get out of would be highlighted within the divorce procedure," Boucher said. "But the divorce law doesn't take into account the fact that he was a criminal."

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said it had begun a consultation to reform the law so "family courts meet the needs of domestic abuse victims".

Boucher, a mother from Chiselborough, said Rogers had come into her life in "a whirlwind" in 2017 and the pair got married two years later.

It was once they were married that things started to "take a turn", she said, and "some very extreme behaviour started to happen".

"It creeps up on you and you're in it, and so you don't kind of notice what is happening."

Boucher said she had ended up "shutting down emotionally" and "cutting off from everyone" because she feared what would happen.

"You find that you're trapped within a situation that you can't get out of."

News.title: Channel 4 to cut 340 jobs by the end of the year in major shake-up
News.content:
Channel 4 has said it plans to cut 340 jobs before the end of the year, reducing its workforce by more than a quarter.

The network, which broadcasts Gogglebox and The Great British Bake Off, will lose around 28% of its current 1,270 staff following a strategic review of the organisation.

Priya Dogra, Channel 4's chief executive, said the announcement "marks the first phase of our transformation, ensuring Channel 4 is the right shape and size to deliver its future strategy and focus investment in the programmes audiences love".

Caroline Dinenage, chair of the culture, media and sport committee said the news would be "deeply worrying for the talented and dedicated people who work at Channel 4".

The network said it planned to focus on creating a simpler and more efficient operating model and enable greater investment in distinctive programming.

In her statement, Dogra said: "Channel 4 is a precious asset which plays a unique role in the UK.

"We need to secure and own our future so we can continue to make shows others won't, reach audiences others can't, and thrive as a distinctive and disruptive British voice for future generations.

"The challenges we face require a fundamental transformation in how we work. I know the proposals we are announcing today will be very difficult for many colleagues and will have a significant impact across the organisation."

She added: "These decisions have not been taken lightly, but I strongly believe they are necessary to create a simpler, more focused and more sustainable Channel 4."

News.title: Home with hundreds of thousands of cockroaches like a horror movie, pest controller says
News.content:
Hundreds of thousands of cockroaches were found in a shared home in an infestation described as the worst the pest controller had seen in 38 years.

Gareth Davies, who said the scene had looked like one from a "Stephen King film", said his team had used specialist equipment to vacuum up "hundreds of thousands" of cockroaches from the four bedroom property in Pontypridd, south Wales.

He said his company had dealt with hundreds of cockroach jobs in the past 12 months, compared with just a handful a year five years ago.

There have been reports of a rise in cockroach sightings across some of Britain's urban areas, according to the British Pest Control Association (BPCA).

The recent warmer weather is thought by some experts to be speeding up cockroaches' breeding cycle.

News.title: Man shot by police after woman stabbed at property
News.content:
A man has been shot by police after a woman was stabbed at a property in Luton.

Shots were fired by armed officers at an address in Cardigan Street at about 12:50 BST on Tuesday.

The man was struck in the arm and leg after a Bedfordshire Police officer discharged four shots, while another fired a baton round.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it was now investigating the police response.

"We have secured the police firearms for examination and CCTV and officers' body worn video have been viewed," a spokesman said.

The man's injuries were described as life-changing but not life-threatening.

Both he and the woman, whose injuries were also not life-threatening, were taken to hospital for treatment.

Bedfordshire Police said it was responding to reports that a man was threatening a woman with a knife at the address.

Det Ch Supt Zara Brown said officers "responded quickly" to the unfolding incident.

"As part of this response, shots were fired by police, and one man sustained serious injuries," she continued.

"Immediate first aid was provided, and he has been taken to hospital, where he remains under police watch."

The force pledged to provide further information about the IOPC investigation when possible.

News.title: Shane Richie pleads not guilty to drink-driving
News.content:
EastEnders actor Shane Richie has pleaded not guilty to a single charge of drink-driving.

The 62-year-old, who has played Alfie Moon in the BBC soap on and off since 2002, was arrested at a petrol station in Harlow, Essex, on 29 July where he was with his Hyundai IX35.

Richie, from Tadworth in Surrey, has appeared at Colchester Magistrates' Court via video link from a hotel room.

The actor - who appeared under his real name of Shane Roche - spoke only to confirm his name, address and plea. He is next due to appear for trial at the same court on 17 November 2027.

News.title: Thousands of teens missing education 'under the radar' of official stats, report warns
News.content:
There could be tens of thousands more teenagers who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) than official statistics suggest, the children's commissioner for England has warned.

A report by Dame Rachel de Souza said around 42,000 16- and 17-year-olds in England were officially classed as studying at college, but were not showing up at least half of the time.

She said they had gone "under the radar" and were "not getting the support that they need".

The Department for Education (DfE) said it planned to help colleges track attendance and ultimately to gather that data centrally.

Unlike schools, further education and sixth form colleges in England are not required to collect or report attendance data.

Dame Rachel's report is based on attendance data obtained from 262 college groups in England and says rates are "substantially lower" than in schools.

It suggests that more than half (52.2%) of 16- and 17-year-olds are estimated to be persistently absent by the standards used in schools, meaning they are missing 10% or more of college sessions.

And around 42,000 (5.9%) are severely absent, meaning they are missing at least half of college sessions.

The DfE estimates that 57,000 16- and 17-year-olds in England are Neet, and Dame Rachel's report argues that these persistently absent teenagers should be considered as "hidden" Neets alongside them.

Dame Rachel told the BBC a range of factors led to teenagers missing college, including part-time work and travel costs, and that some had been largely absent from education since the Covid pandemic.

She said while those juggling part-time employment were likely to miss college every so often, it was those who are "far more vulnerable" who were likely to be severely absent.

She added that it was "shocking" that the DfE did not collect the data as it meant the issue was "ignored".

"It's under the radar and these kids are not getting the support that they need," she said.

Apple has launched the iPhone Duo, its most dramatic redesign ever.

The new device brings two screens to the phone: one on the outside, and then a larger one when it is unfolded like a book.

open image in gallery ( Apple )

The new look also brings a host of new software features, including the option to use multiple apps at once.

Many of Apple’s competitors have been selling foldable devices for years. But new chief executive John Ternus suggested that many of those were simply like two phones stuck together – and that it had taken extra time to ensure that the new device actually made use of its multiple and larger screens.

open image in gallery ( Apple )

The company wanted to avoid the “distracting” crease that can be seen in the middle of other folding phones, for instance, as well as the problems with durability that can be found in rival devices. Apple said that it had used new technology that ensures that the fold cannot be seen when the phone is open, and will be able to resist scratching and breaking.

The phone also features many of the same upgrades that were introduced in the iPhone 18 Pro, which Apple launched earlier in the same event. That includes the new A20 Pro chip, for instance, which adds better performance including for AI.

News.title: Tate brothers lose bid for release from Miami jail amid UK extradition fight
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

Andrew and Tristan Tate must remain in custody in Miami as they fight extradition to the United Kingdom, where the brothers are accused of rape and sex trafficking, a federal judge ruled on Wednesday.

US Magistrate Lauren Louis denied a defense motion for release, meaning the Tates will remain jailed during a potentially lengthy extradition process that could take months.

Miami federal judge Louis stated in her ruling that the Tates “have failed to meet their burden to demonstrate that they do not present a risk of flight or danger to the community, or that special circumstances warrant their release. Respondents have failed to demonstrate that special circumstances here warrant relief, whether their proposed special circumstances are considered singly or together.

"Having failed to meet these three factors, Respondents’ Motion for Release Pending Extradition Proceedings is DENIED.”

open image in gallery The brothers are fighting against extradition to the UK ( Reuters )

The brothers’ legal team said in a statement that the decision to keep them in custody creates a legal contradiction. The Tates are being detained in the United States because of a British extradition request while simultaneously being required to defend themselves against charges in Romania, the statement said.

“They are now facing an extraordinary situation in which they are being held thousands of miles from Romania while Romanian proceedings continue, deadlines approach, an additional indictment is said to be imminent and their own Romanian lawyer says he cannot properly prepare,” the lawyers said.

“No serious person can pretend that this can be reviewed properly through occasional conversations from a federal detention center in another country.”

Andrew Tate, 39, and Tristan Tate, 38, who are dual US-British citizens, have become among the world’s most polarising internet personalities with their promotion of wealth, male dominance and misogyny through their social media empire. Prosecutors say the brothers are a flight risk because they appear to have money and have bragged about multiple passports.

During a hearing last month in Miami, the brothers denied criminal accusations spanning several countries, blasted their critics and described their brash online personas as characters and not their true personalities. The Tates said they exaggerate their claims of wealth to boost their clout on social media.

The new allegations are the latest in the Tates’ long-running international legal saga spanning the U.S., Britain and Romania. They have been held at the Federal Detention Center in Miami since making a brief court appearance two days after their July 18 arrest.

Lawyers for the Tates asked the judge to allow them to be freed from custody at least until an extradition hearing can be held on their UK rape and trafficking charges.

open image in gallery The Tate brothers are avid fans of Donald Trump ( AFP/Getty )

They have repeatedly argued that Britain’s request is out of line because their criminal case in Romania is going first. Romanian officials have let the brothers remain free until the proceedings conclude, and they have not tried to flee and are complying with all court restrictions. Earlier this month, Romanian prosecutors indicted the brothers on additional charges.

Andrew Tate is a former professional kickboxer and self-described misogynist who has amassed more than 10 million followers, most of them boys and young men, on X. He has been banned from platforms like YouTube, TikTok and Instagram for violating hate speech guidelines.

He also runs an online academy where he says he teaches young men how to get rich and attract women. Tristan Tate is also a former kickboxer.

The brothers are avid supporters of US president Donald Trump.

News.title: Liverpool v Atletico Madrid LIVE: Bradley Barcola makes first Reds start in Champions League opener
News.content:
Why Liverpool NEED Bradley Barcola

Liverpool begin their Champions League campaign with Atletico Madrid visiting Anfield in gameweek one of the league phase.

The Reds will have aspirations of reaching Madrid in next year’s final, eight years after their sixth European crown in a 2-0 win over Tottenham Hotspur at the Metropolitano. But after swapping in Andoni Iraola, a significant improvement is required after back-to-back champions Paris Saint-Germain dispatched them 4-0 on aggregate in the quarter-finals.

Bradley Barcola made his debut in the 2-0 win at Ipswich last week, following a £125m move from PSG, and Alexander Isak is up and running with a quick-fire double providing the inspiration for the victory.

Diego Simeone’s side lost in last year’s semi-finals to Arsenal in a tense tie, but the Julian Alvarez transfer saga has left a shadow over the beginning of their season after a move to Barcelona or Arsenal failed to materialise.

The two sides faced each other in the same fixture last term, with a 3-2 win for the Reds providing the foundation to advance straight to the last 16 with a top-eight finish. Follow all of the latest from the clash with our live blog below:

News.title: Napoli v Arsenal LIVE: Arteta’s side begin Champions League quest with tricky test in Italy
News.content:
Copa Independent | Why the Premier League's financial might still can't bully Europe's giants in the Champions League

Arsenal begin their Champions League quest with a tricky test against Napoli as Mikel Arteta’s side look to go one better than last year.

The Premier League winners so nearly completed a double with success in Europe in May, falling short in the final against Paris Saint-Germain. The challenge now is to improve again for another continental trophy tilt – and while they may have missed out on a marquee forward, Arteta certainly has plenty of strength and depth at his disposal as they embark on a new European campaign.

Things are unlikely to be straightforward in Naples, though, particularly after travel chaos delayed Arsenal’s arrival in the city. The hosts may have made a slow start in Serie A, and be without Scott McTominay due to a heart issue, but the visitors can expect a hostile reception and a strong Napoli side.

Arizona’s Grand Canyon National Park announced a recovery plan for the canyon’s water system Tuesday as search operations continue following August’s deadly flash flooding.

River patrols are still trying to find one hiker along the Colorado River, which runs through the canyon, officials said in a statement.

Timothy Smith, a 53-year-old Texan and father of three, is the last person who remains unaccounted for after the flooding. He was supposed to return home Wednesday, his wife Carrie Smith wrote in a Tuesday Facebook post.

“These last nine days have been the hardest days that my family has endured,” Carrie wrote.

Park officials confirmed the deaths of Smith’s friends, 46-year-old John Guisti and 42-year-old Brent Rosenkranz, around the river on September 1.

open image in gallery The search continues for Texas hiker Timothy Smith (top right) following deadly flash flooding in Arizona’s Grand Canyon National Park last month ( Family handout )

The hikers were caught off guard by a deluge on August 29 that flooded the park’s Bright Angel Canyon and Phantom Ranch areas with five feet of water.

The fast-moving storm dumped nearly an inch of rain per hour there, forcing the dramatic helicopter evacuations of 80 people.

The flooding rain damaged 40 percent of the park’s main water supply system along the canyon’s South Rim, leading to water cuts for locals and forcing the closure of local hotels.

But now, the park says there is a path forward to restore water service - and it is expected to take weeks, instead of months.

open image in gallery People cross a bridge amid flash flooding in Arizona’s Grand Canyon on August 29. A fast-moving storm forced the rescue of 80 people and killed two men ( Reuters )

open image in gallery The campsite at Bright Angel Creek corridor is seen after it was hit by the flash flood on August 31. People were on nearby trails and campsites ( AFP/Getty )

Crews are working on a temporary pipeline to replace the one destroyed in the flooding. The new pipeline would have the same capacity as the previous pipeline, pumping approximately 500 gallons of water per minute.

“Engineers are in the canyon designing the temporary intake, the existing Transcanyon Waterline contract has been modified to support the work, and construction activities are beginning this week,” the park said.

The park is working with Arizona’s Department of Environmental Quality to meet federal water quality requirements and said teams were actively monitoring the system for leaks and unusual water use.

Officials also stressed that conservation remains “critical” while work moves forward. Every gallon saved by businesses, visitors and locals gives crews more time.

open image in gallery Park members hike through the Grand Canyon South Rim’s Phantom Ranch area on September 5. Park officials say there’s a plan to restore the canyon’s water system, which was damaged in the flooding ( NPS Photo )

Bottled water is being passed out and handwashing stations and portable showers and toilets have been deployed throughout the community.

Tap water remains safe to use and there is no boil-water advisory in effect.

“Current conservation measures are offsetting approximately 137,000 gallons of potable water use each day, extending the amount of time available for crews to complete critical work on the water system,” the park wrote.

News.title: Trump wants to keep non-citizens out of 2030 Census in massive shakeup that could reshape America
News.content:

Donald Trump’s administration is proposing major changes to the upcoming Census that could end up reshaping Congress and how vital public dollars are distributed to the states.

A draft proposal, published Wednesday, would prohibit all noncitizens without a green card from participating in the 2030 Census. That would exclude refugees, people seeking asylum and other protected immigrants with legal status, as well as undocumented people who have long been included in the nation’s headcount.

If the proposed changes survive impending legal challenges, excluding U.S. residents in the once-a-decade population would cut down the government’s official population numbers, figures that are used to determine congressional seats and federal funds that support critical public services.

The changes under Trump, who has been accused of trying to weaponize the U.S. Census Bureau to expand his anti-immigration agenda and boost Republican districts, would disproportionately target Democratic states and cities with large immigrant populations.

The administration also wants to stop asking people about their race and ethnicity, questions that have been included since the first count was performed more than 200 years ago. The Census would also ban questions about Americans’ sexual orientation, questions that the government claims are about “immaterial personal characteristics.”

open image in gallery The Trump administration is once again proposing excluding noncitizens and other immigrants from the once-a-decade Census in a shakeup that could hit states with large immigrant populations hard ( AFP/Getty )

“These proposals are intended to ensure fidelity to the Constitution, improve and protect the core decennial census data, and promote efficiency,” according to the draft.

Under the 14th Amendment of the Constitution, the U.S. must include the "whole number of persons in each state.” It does not mention immigration status.

The proposal claims “illegal aliens (among others) should not be included in the apportionment count, as they are not true inhabitants, members of the body politic, or persons with a ‘usual residence’ in the United States due to their lack of a sufficient tie and allegiance to the United States,” according to the Trump administration.

Trump mounted similar changes to the Census during his first administration, which pushed the Supreme Court to allow a citizenship question on the 2020 questionnaire.

That effort failed. In a narrow 5-4 decision in 2019, Chief Justice John Roberts called the government’s argument “contrived.”

Civil rights groups have warned that the administration’s proposals could imperil constitutional protections and pose severe risks of discrimination against Americans in violation of the Voting Rights Act.

“The Constitution is clear. Every person living in the United States, regardless of immigration status, must be counted in the census,” New York Attorney General Letitia James said Wednesday.

James, who joined lawsuits to prevent the administration from adding a citizenship question in 2020, said her office is “exploring legal options to fight back again.”

open image in gallery The changes under Trump, who has been accused of trying to weaponize the U.S. Census Bureau to expand his anti-immigration agenda and boost Republican districts, would disproportionately target Democratic states and cities with large immigrant populations ( Reuters )

In addition to informing countless studies about the state of the U.S. using expansive demographic data, the Census is also used to determine how the 435 seats in the House of Representatives are divided among the states.

Electoral College votes that determine the presidency are also based on each state’s House delegation, plus two senators.

If Census results show that a state loses population, it could lose congressional representation — changes that could last at least a decade.

The latest proposal follows Trump’s command in August 2025 directing his administration to develop a “new” census as he launched a nationwide redistricting battle for Republican control of Congress before upcoming midterm elections.

This summer, Trump also relied on a dubious Census Bureau report that claims thousands of noncitizens “voted illegally” in previous elections, part of his crusade to prove he “won” the 2020 presidential election and cast doubt on the legitimacy of elections in Democratic-controlled states.

An unauthored, seven-page report — drafted by people affiliated with the Trump-linked America First Policy Institute think tank — claims that “24,000 Noncitizens voted illegally” and that the final number will “explode” after the bureau finishes processing 32 million other votes, according to Trump. “I WON THE ELECTION!” he wrote at the time.

Top Democrats in Congress are pushing the Census Bureau to immediately rescind the report.

“Donald Trump is a loser and a liar who is misusing government resources to cover up the fact that he lost the 2020 election,” Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, said in a statement last week.

“In the process, he is politicizing and undermining the credibility of the Census, with serious consequences for our country,” Garcia added.

In a letter to the Census Bureau’s deputy under secretary George M. Cook, lawmakers wrote that the report’s publicans threaten to “undermine trust in the independence and credibility of the Bureau.”

“The Bureau has been historically regarded as a public institution that employs rigor and integrity in each of its statistical quality standards and operations,” lawmakers wrote.

England piled more pain on Pakistan at Edgbaston, bowling them out for a paltry 133 before Emilio Gay and Harry Brook carried the hosts further into the ascendancy.

Josh Tongue claimed four for 42 while Ollie Robinson and Jofra Archer shared six wickets as Pakistan’s shake-up since going 2-0 down in the three-match series had minimal impact on their miserable fortunes.

Gay and Brook then made fifties to lift England to 156 for four at stumps on day one, leading by 23 with the promise of more to come on Thursday, despite captain Joe Root being out lbw for the 10th time in 13 innings.

While the floodlights were on all day amid heavy cloud cover for large spells, the pitch was relatively blameless but a Pakistan side with four changes to their side since Lord’s were cowed by England’s on-song seamers.

Robinson was magnificent, conceding just 15 runs in 11 overs, as he went from 99 to 102 Test wickets, while his average of 19.1 is the best post-war of any bowler with more than 100 dismissals.

It was unsurprising he made the breakthrough in his second over after Root opted to field and exploit the overheads, with Saim Ayub brought in for his first first-class appearance since October 2025 unwittingly Robinson’s 100th Test victim.

Ayub, one of the raft of new arrivals when Pakistan banished seven players and two coaches last week, survived one leg-before verdict but not a second, dismissed for a 10-ball duck after missing a lavish drive off Robinson coming round the wicket.

open image in gallery Ollie Robinson celebrates a wicket (PA) ( PA Wire )

Azan Awais and Shan Masood both got into awkward positions from innocuous Archer deliveries and succeeded only in bunting tame catches into the leg-side, while Abdullah Shafique perished to Robinson for the fourth time in five innings after edging low to Dan Lawrence at gully.

When Tongue struck in his first over, obliterating the top of off-stump to send Pakistan captain Babar Azam packing, it meant all of the tourists’ top-five had all been dismissed for single figures – the first time that has happened in the first innings of a Test in England.

Saud Shakeel showed a measure of resistance after being given a reprieve on seven, with Ben Duckett dropping his second catch of the morning at first slip off the luckless Gus Atkinson.

Tongue, though, continued to challenge the stumps and saw off debutants Ghazi Ghori and Mohammad Imran, while Razaullah, the third player making his Pakistan bow, was dismissed from his first ball after lunch as he nicked Robinson to Duckett.

Shakeel’s defiance ended on 43 after a beauty from Tongue uprooted his off-stump, earning a grudging nod from the batter at being beaten all ends up, before Mohammad Abbas and Mohammad Ali put on 26 for the last wicket, the highest partnership of Pakistan’s miserable innings that ended in 33.5 overs.

open image in gallery Josh Tongue celebrates a wicket (PA) ( PA Wire )

Ali weathered a nasty blow on his ankle from Archer but was OK to open the bowling and he made the breakthrough when Duckett’s wild slash took a thick edge and flew chest-height to second slip for 11.

Jordan Cox was pinned lbw by Abbas while England were 39 for three just after tea when 21-year-old Razaullah, operating at around 90mph, thudded into Root’s pads and get the lbw decision in his first over in Test cricket.

But Gay and Brook took the sting out of Pakistan in different ways. While Brook looked to counter-attack, Gay, who came into this Test with his spot under pressure, was initially happy to soak up pressure.

Gay, averaging 23.44 from his first five Tests albeit after batting on a succession of seam bowler-friendly pitches, did capitalise on width with several fluent drives and cuts through the off-side.

He was left writhing in agony when he inside-edged into his left leg but went on to reach his third Test half-century.

However, after a 104-run stand with Brook, Gay’s hopes of a more substantial score to ink himself into England’s plans for the winter went awry when he dragged Razaullah on to his stumps for 60.

Brook moved past 1,000 Test runs against Pakistan in just 14 innings although after haring to 40 off 45 balls, he needed a further 25 deliveries to get to his fifty, struggling late on against Abbas, in particular, before surviving to stumps on 52 not out.
