“Like during the international break, we play four games in 10 or 11 days, so it’s not easy. But you have to try to squeeze in a few days here and there and give your mind a bit of a break.”

Sports.title: The three things Arsenal need to do this season to finally win the Champions League - from the players Mikel Arteta must learn to trust to the January transfer window plan and a returning hero
Sports.content:
The Hilton Budapest had been primed, a function room already booked in advance for Arsenal’s staff and players after last season’s Champions League final.

But instead of a raucous party to mark a first European Cup in the club’s 140-year history, a few reflective, sorrows-drowning drinks followed before an early flight back to London for the Premier League title parade through the streets of north London.

The disappointment exuding from Mikel Arteta in the post-match press conference following the defeat on penalties by Paris Saint-Germain was marked. Ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title had gone out the window, his words verged on anger.

‘Pain, that's it, when you are so close in the competition and you are a few penalty kicks away from winning the biggest football club competition, that's the way which you feel,’ he said.

After ending that long, agonising wait to be crowned champions of England, conquering Europe is Arteta's final frontier. The Spaniard has never tasted success in a European competition as a player or manager, and often uses the Champions League as a reference point in how legacies are defined.

Arsenal are well primed to make that final step. They were, after all, only a few kicks from glory in May, and have strengthened further this summer with additions such as Bruno Guimaraes, Christos Tzolis and Ezri Konsa. But how do they get over that final hurdle?

Mikel Arteta's side were a penalty shootout away from finally lifting their first European Cup against Paris Saint-Germain in Budapest in May

Gabriel's decisive miss from the spot was an agonising end to a season that could have been historic

1. Trust the depth

Arsenal’s squad depth gives Arteta the luxury of rotating without necessarily weakening the starting XI.

Ben White has made a case to continue at right back even when Jurrien Timber returns from injury, his telepathic connection with Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard forming a triumvirate which opponents have difficulty stopping on the right flank.

In the middle, Myles Lewis-Skelly has performed well in place of the injured Bruno Guimaraes. The new £75million Brazilian is expected to walk into the line-up on Wednesday against Napoli but after his recent displays, Lewis-Skelly will be on the Brazilian’s heels if there’s any dip in form. It’s a great situation to have for Arteta. But he still needs to utilise it.

Last season, he arguably gave far too many minutes to Declan Rice when he was already tiring, for example. The England midfielder, who went on to play a key role at the World Cup, made 55 appearances in all competitions, with 49 starts and 4,454 minutes, or 91 per cent of Arsenal's minutes when he was available for selection. No Arsenal outfielder played more. Rice himself during the World Cup admitted he had been playing through neural pain in his hamstring since December.

Arsenal had four outfield players above 4,200 minutes - Rice, Martin Zubimendi (4,298), William Saliba (4,254) and Gabriel (4,210). This level of excessive workload must be better shared if Arsenal are to go all the way to the final again, and potentially lift the elusive trophy.

Zubimendi and Rice's back-up, Christian Norgaard, were not trusted to give the Spaniard a rest, but now Lewis-Skelly or Guimaraes can offer that. Konsa can cover while Saliba and Cristhian Mosquera are injured, and Piero Hincapie can slot seamlessly in if Gabriel needs a spell out.

Even Arteta hinted at this in Budapest after the defeat by PSG, saying: ‘You have to get into the competition with all the squad available in the best moment, each player. And we've had more players, many more players than last season but not all of them in that condition for different reasons. And that's something we have to improve as well.’ At least he’s aware. Now he needs to trust those on the bench to get him through.

Declan Rice has spoken of the neural pain he suffered from this summer, and surely cannot keep on playing as many minutes as he did last season

In Myles Lewis-Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes, Arteta has two high-class options he can call on to give Rice a rest

2. Go again in January

Viktor Gyokeres has fallen down the pecking order with Kai Havertz fully fit.

It was always the plan last season, but an injury to Havertz on the opening day at Old Trafford last season resulted in Gyokeres becoming the Gunners’ first-choice striker in the previous campaign, where he struck 21 goals across all competitions after joining for £56million.

The Swede, though, has only made one substitute appearance in three league matches, coming off the bench for 12 minutes against Chelsea on Sunday and showing signs of rust.

After Havertz and Gyokeres, though, Arteta’s options thin out dramatically. Midfielder Mikel Merino could once again be thrown up front to fill the gap, though this would not be ideal. Having failed in their chase for either Vinicius Junior, Julian Alvarez or Lautaro Martinez, Arsenal are very light in the striker position.

It begs the question: can the club lure the likes of Bournemouth’s Eli Junior Kroupi in the January window? He’s a player Arteta admires, has a special place in fans' hearts after scoring the goal that helped seal the title in May and could provide the firepower needed to get Arsenal over the line in Europe too.

Eli Junior Kroupi scored home and away for Bournemouth against Arsenal last season - could he be the missing piece in Arteta's puzzle?

3. Timber's limbering up

The importance of Timber can’t be overstated. In the Budapest defeat, the Dutchman was only half-fit, and came on for an out-of-place Mosquera only after the Spaniard had given away a penalty for a lunge on PSG's Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.

Timber is defensively solid, rarely bypassed by opposition players and commits forward with overlaps, too, in the final third. When fully firing, he is arguably the best right back in the league, and was voted as such in the PFA Team of the Year last season.

The 25-year-old trained on Tuesday morning and is in the squad for Wednesday’s fixture against Napoli.

Timber’s return has been a long, arduous journey from a groin injury which had affected him since March. It ruled him out of the Netherlands’ World Cup squad before returning to light training sessions at the start of Arsenal’s pre-season in July.

If the Gunners can have Timber fully fit for the latter stages of the competition, that is a huge plus.

Sports.title: Michael Carrick admits Man United's derby disadvantage is 'not ideal' with City handed two extra days to prepare - as he outlines Champions League ambitions with Luke Shaw a doubt for opener
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick admits that having two days less than Manchester City to prepare for Sunday’s Old Trafford derby isn’t ‘ideal’ for Manchester United.

While City opened their Champions League campaign with a win in Porto on Tuesday night, United face Sabah of Azerbaijan at Old Trafford in a one-off Thursday slot.

It has given Enzo Maresca more time to work with his squad before the 199th Manchester derby this weekend, and Carrick has no choice but to accept the situation.

‘I'm not concerned,’ said the United head coach. ‘Listen, I wouldn't say it's ideal in some ways, but it's not something that we've given too much thought about.

‘We're not in control of that. We've got to deal with the cards that we're dealt and that's what it is, so we'll make the most of it.’

Carrick is waiting to make a decision over Luke Shaw’s availability for the next two games after the veteran defender missed training at Carrington on Wednesday.

While City opened their Champions League campaign with a win in Porto on Tuesday night, United face Sabah of Azerbaijan at Old Trafford in a one-off Thursday slot

Carrick is waiting to make a decision over Luke Shaw’s availability for the next two games after the veteran defender missed training at Carrington on Wednesday

The club said it was a designated day off, but Carrick admitted it was a decision taken after Shaw played in United’s 2-2 draw at Everton on Sunday.

His absence raised concerns that United’s decision not to sign left-back cover for the 31-year-old England defender before the transfer window closed last week could backfire on them.

‘We just gave Luke an extra recovery day,’ added Carrick. ‘We'll see by tomorrow how he is, but it's not an ongoing thing or a plan or anything like that. It was just off the back of the game the other day.

‘So, as normal, each individual has different little things that we manage, and Luke was one of them today.’

United decided against signing cover for Shaw in the transfer window despite showing interest in Newcastle’s Lewis Hall and rejecting an opportunity to sign Rayan Ait-Nouri on loan from Manchester City on deadline day.

The 31-year-old veteran defender started every Premier League game for United last season, but it was widely accepted that he could not go another season without injury. Shaw was replaced by Noussair Mazraoui in added time during Sunday’s 2-2 draw at Everton after setting up a goal for Benjamin Sesko, but it was assumed the change was tactical.

United are relying on a number of back-up options if Shaw is unavailable, with Patrick Dorgu able to play at left back after being used in a more advanced role under Carrick.

Both right-backs, Mazraoui and Diogo Dalot, are capable of playing on the opposite flank, and academy product Harry Amass has stayed at the club when it was anticipated he would leave. New £70million midfield Carlos Baleba – currently out until October – could also be used as an auxiliary left-back.

United’s clash with Sabah marks their first appearance in the Champions League for 1,003 days stretching back to December 2023.

Carrick, who played when United last lifted the trophy in Moscow in 2008, insists the club are back where they belong but must be humble considering their recent history in Europe.

Carrick, who played when United last lifted the trophy in Moscow in 2008, insists the club are back where they belong but must be humble considering their recent history in Europe

‘It's a magical competition,’ he said. ‘It's where we all want to be. When you're out of it, you realise how special it is, and when you're in it you want to make the most of it.

‘I think we've all seen some special nights and felt some special things in this competition over the years. It's the best competition to challenge yourself and to push against the best. We're delighted to be here, but we're not here to just enjoy the occasion. We're here to do the business and go as far as we possibly can.

‘Winning the Champions League is the best feeling I've been lucky enough to have as a footballer. For me, it was the ultimate and it would be nice to feel that again some day.

‘It's not something that you can take for granted, what it takes to be there and what it takes to stay there. We've missed out on it for a number of years, and now we're back so I think it means a lot.

‘We've done an awful lot of good work to be here in a short space of time. We want the expectation, that's a privileged position to be in. But I think we've got to be humble enough and realistic enough to know where we're coming from and where we want to get to.’

On facing Sabah, a club that didn’t even exist until 2017, Carrick said: ‘They're a very well-coached team. They've obviously won a lot of football matches over the last 12 months, and so they're playing with a lot of confidence. We’re fully aware of what we're up against and the challenge that we face.’

Sports.title: Newcastle Confidential: Revealed - the key detail in Lewis Hall's new deal, Toon line up contract extensions for long-serving duo, Will Osula injury update, how close NUFC got to signing £85m star and club cash in with two new sponsors
Sports.content:
Newcastle Confidential: Revealed - the key detail in Lewis Hall's new deal, Toon line up contract extensions for long-serving duo, Will Osula injury update, how close NUFC got to signing £85m star and club cash in with two new sponsors

Lewis Hall’s new contract does NOT include a release clause, Confidential can reveal – and that could be bad news for Manchester United.

Hall, 22, was Man United’s top target at left back this summer but he was a player Newcastle had no intention of selling. Omar Berrada, chief executive at Old Trafford, was told by opposite number David Hopkinson that Hall would be going nowhere, and the Red Devils did not attempt to test that resolve thereafter.

Contract talks accelerated last week and an agreement has now been reached, with improved terms and a two-year extension. Lawyers have this week been going over the finer details of the five-year deal – as is the way with all modern contracts – and an announcement is due.

Crucially, there is no release clause in the package, amid suggestion from Manchester that the club will return for Hall next summer.

Their interest is likely to be revisited, but the new contract protects the player’s value and rewards him for his development since joining Newcastle from Chelsea for £35million in 2023, making 102 appearances and scoring three goals.

Hall is set to be included in Thomas Tuchel’s first England squad of the season when he names his players for four Nations League matches next Friday.

Lewis Hall’s new contract does NOT include a release clause, Confidential can reveal - and that could be bad news for Manchester United

The 22-year-old's form for Newcastle has earned him four caps for England, and he is set to be named in Thomas Tuchel's Three Lions squad next week

New deals lined up for Murphy and Willock

Sticking with contracts, talks over extensions for Jacob Murphy and Joe Willock will take place after they stayed at the club beyond the transfer window.

The pair are now in the final year of their current deals but club chiefs will look at extending those terms by 12 months.

Newcastle turned down a £15m offer from Nottingham Forest for Murphy, while Besiktas explored a £17m move for Willock.

New boss Matthias Jaissle sees the value in both players and communicated his wish for them to stay put.

Joe Willock and Jacob Murphy are two of the longest-serving players in Newcastle's squad, having joined in 2021 and 2017 respectively

Osula making good progress

William Osula is out of his protective boot and is now fully mobile as he targets a return to action, which could even be this side of the international break.

Reports in Denmark last week suggested his foot injury – first revealed by Confidential two weeks ago – was far more serious than anticipated and claimed the striker was set for an extended spell on the sidelines. We can allay those fears by revealing there has been no fracture and there is no need for surgery.

Indeed, Osula is now able to work on rebuilding his fitness at the training ground and staff are pushing to have him involved before next weekend’s visit of Hull City, the final fixture ahead of the three-week break. The more likely target, say sources, is the first game after the international matches at Coventry City on October 12.

However, news that the 23-year-old has not suffered a serious injury will be welcomed by supporters and head coach Matthias Jaissle, who has only had the Dane available to him for 56 minutes of this campaign so far.

Meanwhile, staff were today assessing the severity of the hamstring injury that forced off Amar Dedic at Millwall on Tuesday night. The early indications are that the problem is not serious.

Newcastle staff staff are pushing to have Will Osula involved before next weekend’s visit of newly promoted upstarts Hull City, the final fixture ahead of the three-week break

New man's central demand

Matias Fernandez-Pardo has told Newcastle he wants to start matches as a No 9 – and that is where they intend to play him.

The 21-year-old finished the campaign as a centre forward at Lille, but up until March, he had spent most of his time on the left wing. The season before, he started only once as a striker in Ligue 1.

However, that is the position Fernandez-Pardo spoke about during talks to sign him last month. Now he is in the building, the plan to use him there remains unaltered.

Interestingly, Newcastle’s data analysts returned only two players with the same profile as Anthony Gordon, in terms of their output in both the left wing and central striker roles. One was Fernandez-Pardo, the other was Said El Mala of Cologne. El Mala, 20, did not move this summer, but he remains on Newcastle’s watchlist.

Meanwhile, Pardo’s wish to play as a No 9 will see him compete with Osula for the starting jersey, with Yoane Wissa likely to be used more as a No 10.

Matias Fernandez-Pardo has made clear to the club that he wants to play as a No9

One that got away?

Here is a belated one on transfers – three years later! – but Newcastle spoke with Ayyoub Bouaddi when he was 15 years old.

I only heard this in recent days and thought it was worth sharing after seeing the 18-year-old Moroccan make such an impressive start at Manchester City, whom he joined for £85.6m from Lille last month.

The midfielder and his family, I’m told, had conversations with club staff with a view to building a relationship.

However, they were not the only club to do so, and Bouaddi had his pick of several major European sides this summer after a stellar World Cup.

Newcastle made contact with Man City's new midfield gem Ayyoub Bouaddi three years ago, when he was in Lille's academy

Show me the money!

Finally, Newcastle will confirm a new multi-million-pound partnership with Coca-Cola this week.

The global drinks brand will replace Sela as sponsor of the St James’ STACK fan zone.

Newcastle have also signed a new multi-year deal to extend their partnership with betting and entertainment brand, BetMGM.

Negotiated by chief executive Hopkinson, the deals represent another step in the club’s drive to increase commercial revenues. More partnership announcements are expected in the coming months.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi is set to buy Spanish second-division club Eldense - as Argentina icon continues to grow his footballing empire while still playing
Sports.content:
Lionel Messi is set to buy Spanish second-division club Eldense - as Argentina icon continues to grow his footballing empire while still playing

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Lionel Messi has reached an agreement in principle to become the owner of second-division Spanish side Eldense, Daily Mail Sport can confirm.

Messi is set to acquire the shares currently held by Colombian investment group Grupo TH, making him the club's majority shareholder.

The deal is expected to be finalised in the coming days once the final legal and contractual procedures are completed and it has received approval from Spain's High Council for Sport (CSD). The financial terms of the transaction have not been disclosed.

The Valencia-based outfit were promoted to the second division at the end of last season and have faced a difficult start to their campaign, picking up two points in the opening four games. Their coach Claudio Barragan was sacked earlier this week, leaving the club without a manager.

Messi's acquisition of Eldense marks the latest venture in the 39-year-old Argentinian star's growing football empire.

A few months ago Messi purchased a 100 per cent stake in another Spanish side, UE Cornella, a semi-professional outfit located on the outskirts of Barcelona.

UE Cornella, founded in 1951, play in Spain's fifth tier, and the club said Messi's arrival 'marked the beginning of a new chapter in its history, aimed at driving both sporting and institutional growth, strengthening its foundations and continuing to invest in talent'.

Lionel Messi has reached an agreement in principle to become the owner of second-division Spanish side Eldense, Daily Mail Sport can confirm

View this post on Instagram

They added: 'The project is guided by a long-term vision and a strategic plan that combines ambition, sustainability, and a strong connection to its local roots.'

Messi, who recently announced his international retirement following Argentina's defeat in the World Cup final, has further investments elsewhere, although neither matches the scale of his two Spanish investments.

He co-owns Uruguay side Deportivo LSM alongside Inter Miami team-mate Luis Suarez. He also holds a direct equity option in his MLS team, Inter Miami, which allows him to buy a partial ownership stake in the club after his playing career ends.

As his empire grows, however, he could face a potential stumbling block.

Eldense and Cornella are currently separated by three divisions, but it is unlikely the Royal Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) would allow both teams to compete in the same division if the two clubs were ever to reach that point.

Eldense, founded in 1921, have spent most of their history outside the top two divisions of Spanish football.

They were promoted to the second tier for the first time since 1964 in 2023, suffered relegation in 2025 and secured an immediate return this past summer.

They play their home games at the Nuevo Pepico Amat, a 5,776-capacity stadium in the city of Elda.

Sports.title: Sea Of Rain ready to repay faith at Doncaster... plus our top tips for Day One of the St Leger Festival
Sports.content:
Connections of recent purchase Sea Of Rain are eyeing a swift return on their investment in Thursday's Betfred May Hill Stakes at Doncaster.

The daughter of Naval Crown, formerly owned by trainer Jim Bolger, created such a good impression in the Newtownanner Stud Irish EBF Stakes 12 days ago that the race sponsors snapped up the talented filly to run in the colours of the Clonmel based Maurice Regan-owned stud farm.

Regarded by Bolger as ‘my Oaks filly for next year’, Sea Of Rain saw out the mile strongly at the Curragh when springing an 18/1 surprise in the hands of Colin Keane, although her handler was one of the least shocked by the victory.

‘I intended backing Sea Of Rain when I saw the 25-1, but I forgot to do it. I'm the worst punter in the world,’ said Bolger who this week sold his Coolcullen base to Grand National-winning trainer Emmet Mullins.

‘The performance was no surprise. All she needed was the mile and a proper gallop.’

The ongoing restructuring of Bolger’s training and bloodstock enterprises offered an opportunity for Regan to step in and acquire a filly that, along with Spartan Nua, has held her form during a season where her octogenarian handler has struggled for winners.

‘She put up a good performance in the Group Three and we bought her after that and we’ll find out today if it was good business,’ said PJ Colville, representing the owners.

Sea of Rain en route to victory at the Curragh in August

‘She looks an uncomplicated filly and the mile will suit her well. Good to soft should be fine and we look to have a nice draw near the middle.

‘Charlie Appleby’s horse (Musical Times) will be tough to beat and she looks really promising, but after that it looks fairly open.

‘It’s another step up again, but we think she’s up to it. She’s been learning on the job and her last run was her best run so far and that is always a positive.’

As Bolger bids to land one of Thursday's feature events, the ambitious Mullins is targeting Group 2 glory of his own on Friday when recent Ffos Las winner Winday takes a sizeable step up in class in the Betfred Howard Wright Doncaster Cup Stakes.

The son of Galiway returned from a spell hurdling in France to win by a wide margin on his Welsh comeback and, as a three-year-old without a penalty for any pattern race success, will carry a whopping 16lb less than ante-post favourite Caballo De Mar.

Sports.title: Man City star Erling Haaland opens up on heated scenes during Porto Champions League clash - and claims his opponent 'grabbed my bottom'
Sports.content:
Man City star Erling Haaland opens up on heated scenes during Porto Champions League clash - and claims his opponent 'grabbed my bottom'

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Erling Haaland has opened up on the heated scenes that occurred towards the end of Man City's Champions League victory over Porto on Tuesday.

Haaland, who scored twice in the 2-0 win, was cautioned after tussling with Pablo Rosario late in the game and claims that the midfielder wanted to stop him by any means necessary.

‘I was really keen on a hat-trick and it seemed like he [Rosario] was very eager to stop me from getting it,’ Haaland told TV 2. ‘It was a little interesting, that. You'll be seeing a picture where he's grabbing my bottom... it’ll be interesting to see that picture.’

That was not the only flashpoint of the match, with both sets of players having to be dragged away from each other in the tunnel at half time.

City reserve goalkeeper Marcus Bettinelli is understood to have been pushed by Porto officials after the home team were incensed by refereeing decisions.

UEFA’s disciplinary committee are assessing reports by the match delegate and referee Szymon Marciniak to ascertain whether any action is necessary. The punishment for any guilty party is likely to amount to a fine.

Erling Haaland has opened up on his tussle with Pablo Rosario during Man City's Champions League victory over Porto on Tuesday

Haaland scored twice during the 2-0 triumph, including a header shortly after half-time

Haaland also spoke about his recent flurry of headed goals and said they have come from perfecting the art with his father in the garden.

The City striker managed to score six headers last season but now has three in his last three matches – including the first of a brace in Porto.

HAALAND BY NUMBERS His incredible goalscoring record in club football: Left foot - 221 goals Right foot - 43 goals Head - 37 goals Other - 1 goal TOTAL: 302 goals

Haaland pinpointed his aerial ability as something to improve after sealing a move to the Etihad Stadium in 2022 and believes it has now added another string to his bow.

And the dedication has extended to impromptu sessions with Alfie Haaland at home in Cheshire, seemingly recreating scenes of his childhood.

‘Over the years, I’ve worked a lot on my heading,’ Haaland said. ‘I’ve improved it massively and it’s become a strength of my game. I think a lot of it comes down to experience.'

Haaland has 37 career headed goals in club football, just over 10 per cent of his overall haul and added: ‘Actually, two days ago I was practising headers with my dad in the garden.'

Sports.title: Steve Borthwick's new contract beggars belief and smacks of England having no long-term plan. No matter how the RFU spin it as they hide from tough questions, this is why their logic is so flawed, writes NIK SIMON
Sports.content:
However the RFU decides to present it, the decision to extend Steve Borthwick’s contract as England head coach will go down like a lead balloon.

Conor O’Shea, the governing body’s executive director of performance rugby, quietly slipped the news into a BBC podcast. Perhaps it was a futile attempt to take the sting out of any upcoming formal announcement.

Borthwick has been handed a short-term extension until the middle of 2028, which effectively puts him in charge of the first Six Nations campaign after next year’s World Cup.

It is hardly a leap of faith by the decision makers at Twickenham. In Ireland, their union handed Andy Farrell a four-year contract extension to keep him in Dublin. Now that is an indication of how you really back your coach.

England should have moved heaven and earth to bring Farrell back to the RFU for next year. He guided the Lions to a series victory in Australia last year but Bill Sweeney, the RFU CEO, did not even make contact.

The RFU’s token gesture to extend Borthwick’s contract for a few months smacks of an organisation which does not have a long-term plan.

Contract extensions are typically a reward for success but this is a decision that leaves more questions than answers.

O’Shea told the BBC podcast that he has a ‘long list’ of candidates to lead England through their next World Cup cycle, yet most rivals have already identified their man.

Steve Borthwick has been offered a new contract to take him through the 2028 Six Nations

England have lost five of their eight Tests this year, including their worst ever Six Nations

Borthwick has won 58 per cent of his games since he took over from Eddie Jones in 2022. Jones, for the record, was marched out of Twickenham with a winning record of 73 per cent.

The optics of renewing Borthwick’s contract in a year when England finished the Six Nations in fifth place are not good.

The 2026 Championship was England’s worst ever, including a first defeat by Italy. Borthwick’s critics are still coming to terms with the fact that he was not sacked after that campaign. Now, he has been backed by Sweeney and O’Shea further. It really does beggar belief.

You do not have to look far on social media to see that Borthwick’s stock with the public is low, despite his victories over Fiji and Argentina this summer.

He has been lambasted for his lack of public emotion – although there were signs of change there when he snapped in his last press conference after his team’s final July Test.

‘I love it. You’re my negativity committee. It’s lovely coming in and talking to you again,’ he said, when I asked about the four yellow cards conceded by England during the second half of their victory over Argentina.

The recent Tests between South Africa and New Zealand were a step up in quality and intensity from the Nations Championship, highlighting the gulf that has formed in the Test arena.

In many ways, this latest RFU decision feels like nothing more than a move to take some of the heat off Borthwick in the upcoming autumn campaign, rather than challenging him to take the best-funded rugby union in the world back to the top of the sport.

Questions remain about the national team’s playing style, with a jarring contrast between Borthwick’s philosophy and the attacking flair of his Northampton-dominated backline.

This latest decision by Bill Sweeney's RFU feels like nothing more than a move to take some of the heat off Borthwick in the upcoming autumn campaign

England are only six months on from losing to Italy for the first time, and still have four tricky autumn fixtures to navigate before another Six Nations campaign and then the World Cup

If England fail to impress against Australia in their next Test at Twickenham, the dreaded boos will not be far away. That was what did for Jones in the end, leading to Borthwick taking on the role a year out from the 2023 World Cup.

Since then, despite a 12-match winning run last year, it is hard to make the argument England have progressed significantly.

‘You don't want them (coaches) looking for a job going into (a World Cup),’ O'Shea explained. ‘Everyone knows it will be judged on the World Cup, but you can't have a group of coaches going in with that uncertainty, especially when you look at the timing. So, we will give that certainty and that will give us time to look properly.’

But Borthwick already has the job of his dreams, so why would he be looking elsewhere? His entire focus should be on winning the World Cup and earning a genuine contract extension.

But unless England miraculously lift the Webb Ellis Cup in Sydney, then it is hard to see a swing in the opinion polls. That looks a long shot at best right now. On the evidence of recent weeks, they look far behind the standards being set by the Springboks and All Blacks.

You suspect the likes of Jacques Nienaber and Ronan O’Gara are already plotting their next move, rather than waiting until spring 2028 for a call from Twickenham.

O’Gara looks most likely to stay with his French employers La Rochelle, perhaps with a view to one day succeeding Farrell in his homeland. England could do worse than look at Nienaber, currently with Leinster.

Could Shaun Edwards, one of the world's best and most decorated coaches who has been overlooked by England for so long while winning trophies with their rivals, one day come into the picture too?

Jacques Nienaber (left) is one of the masterminds of South Africa's back-to-back World Cup wins and should be squarely in England's thoughts to lead them into the 2031 tournament

Borthwick already has the job of his dreams, so why would he be looking elsewhere? His entire focus should be on winning the World Cup and earning a genuine contract extension

Borthwick’s assistants Lee Blackett and Richard Wigglesworth will already be thinking about jobs with more responsibility after next year’s World Cup.

Funnily enough, O’Shea accidentally walked into an England press conference on the day he recorded said podcast.

‘Wrong room,’ he declared, before performing one of the sharpest U-turns of the year.

Perhaps it makes sense now, because the RFU’s latest decision is one that is particularly tricky to explain.

Sports.title: Revealed: The staggering sums of money LIV golfers - including Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau - are owed following collapse of Saudi-backed rebel league
Sports.content:
Revealed: The staggering sums of money LIV golfers - including Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau - are owed following collapse of Saudi-backed rebel league

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

LIV Golf's high-profile stars are waiting to collect more than £30million in unpaid money from the Saudi-backed rebel league after it filed for bankruptcy on Tuesday.

A 'Chapter 11' petition was lodged in New Jersey last night, with the breakaway league locked in a battle for survival ever since its Saudi Arabian backers announced in April that they were pulling the plug.

Although the latest development had been widely expected, it marks a significant milestone in LIV's dramatic downfall, coming four years after its arrival triggered an ugly civil war in the sport.

The 'Chapter 11' petition also revealed the staggering sums owed to LIV's golfers, who are listed among the league's unsecured creditors.

Jon Rahm tops the list with a huge $7.5million (£5.5m) outstanding, followed by Bryson DeChambeau, who is owed $5.8m (£4.3m).

Dustin Johnson, Cameron Smith and Adrian Meronk are owed $5.5m (£4.1m), $4.8m (£3.5m) and $4.4m (£3.2m) respectively, while English golfer Tyrrell Hatton has $3.4m (£2.5m) in unsecured claims.

LIV Golf's high-profile stars are waiting to collect more than £30million in unpaid money - Jon Rahm, pictured, tops the list with a huge $7.5million (£5.5m) outstanding in unsecured claims

The sums detailed in the petition refer to money already owed to the golfers as of the date of the filing, rather than the full value of their respective LIV contracts.

Rahm's mammoth LIV contract was agreed at a reported $350m (£258m), which means the £5.5m currently outstanding represents only a fraction of the enormous deal he signed to join the breakaway league.

While bankruptcy might allow the circuit to realise its stated ambition of a LIV 2.0, it remains to be seen if their forthcoming union with BC Partners, a private equity group, will be sufficient for the league to extend into a 2027 season.

The greatest unknown at this stage is which of their marquee players will stay with the project in a vastly diminished and less lucrative form, as it is understood that bankruptcy will allow the golfers to exit their contracts, even if they have time still to run.

Any LIV golfers looking to return to the PGA Tour could face a fresh battle for reinstatement, with the American circuit having already imposed significant financial penalties on players who defected to its Saudi-backed rival.

Earlier this year, Rahm appeared to hedge his bets by making peace with the PGA Tour, agreeing to return for occasional appearances and pay the fines he had accrued since joining LIV in 2024.

Bryson DeChambeau, whose LIV deal expired at the end of the 2026 season, is owed £4.3m

Yasir Al Rumayyan (Governor of PIF, Chairman of Aramco) congratulates winning player, Elvis Smylie (Ripper GC) on day 4 of LIV Golf in Riyadh LIV Golf Riyad back in February

'The DP World Tour (PGA European Tour) and Jon Rahm have come to an agreement on conditional releases to play in conflicting tournaments on LIV Golf during the remainder of its 2026 season,' a spokesperson from the league said. Meanwhile, Rahm revealed there was 'no longer a standoff' and that concessions were made by both parties.

DeChambeau's deal expired at the end of the 2026 season but he is expected to recommit in return for equity in the league. The picture around Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton is far more concerning to LIV insiders - both men are contracted through 2028 and Daily Mail Sport sources had indicated prior to bankruptcy that both men were likely to leave in the event of the petition being filed.

Rahm, for one, hinted at the possibility earlier on Tuesday, when asked at the DP World Tour's Irish Open if he would like to see a pathway back to the PGA Tour. He said: 'I still have a contract with LIV 1.0 that I am more than willing to fulfil, so like I said time will tell.'

The choice of phrase - 'LIV 1.0' – would suggest his loyalty was contingent on his existing terms being honoured in order to continue with LIV.

Sports.title: There should be no easy way back for LIV rebels but Rory McIlroy has given them hope
Sports.content:
There should be no easy way back for LIV rebels but Rory McIlroy has given them hope

The Saudi-funded tour has filed for bankruptcy protection and will be relaunched on a smaller scale which will mean an exodus of its top stars

View 3 Images Jon Rahm looks certain to leave LIV Golf after it filed for bankruptcy protection (Image: Getty Images)

On more than one occasion, Rory McIlroy has had no hesitation in putting the boot into the LIV Golf rebels, especially as the Saudis came to realise their project was a monumental white elephant.

‌



You’ve made your bed on an obscene pile of dollars, now lie in it, was his gist. That even applied to Ryder Cup mates such as Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton.

‌



But the fact he appeared to be in a more conciliatory mood when discussing LIV Golf filing for bankruptcy protection could hint at a compromise that might eventually see the world’s best players competing against each other on a more regular basis. That is what golf fans would love to see.

‌



Rory McIlroy clarifies Eric Trump 'friend' claim and role in giving Donald dream opportunity READ MORE :

Jon Rahm faces up to LIV Golf uncertainty and PGA Tour return as Irish fans wait READ MORE :

With the four majors finished by the middle of July - and the PGA Tour’s FedEx Cup wrapped up by the end of August - there are long stretches of the global golf schedule that feature tournaments of limited worldwide interest. And that is what the recently-announced, fresh alliance between the PGA Tour and the DP World Tour (formerly the European Tour) has promised to address.

The bottom line is that the PGA Tour does not need to welcome back the LIV golfers. Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau might make their product a touch more compelling, but from a fan's point of view, they are probably the only two who would make a difference.

With the DP World Tour, it is different. Their best players move to the PGA Tour as a matter of course and career progression. The DP World Tour would be stronger and more attractive with the best LIV golfers in it.

‌



View 3 Images Rory McIlroy has said LIV Golf's struggles could be good for the game (Image: Richard Heathcote/Getty Images)

A measured McIlroy explained it well, saying: “I would predict that you will see some (LIV) guys leave. They are free to now as, I guess, contracts have been breached by them filing for bankruptcy.

“I think that means other tours have decisions to make. Obviously, there are a lot of players on LIV that can strengthen golf tournaments and make them more competitive.

‌



"So I would see that as a good thing for the DP World Tour. Overall, I think the way things are working out, it is a very good thing for the golf ecosystem.”

Over £33million is owed to players by LIV. Rahm is owed £5.5 million, DeChambeau £4.2 million, and Hatton £2.5 million.

View 3 Images Bryson DeChambeau is owed £4.2million by LIV Golf (Image: Jason Butler, Getty Images)

‌



They can walk away from LIV, which is rebranding itself as LIV 2.0 next year, with private, non-Saudi investment. But then, it is a question of whether they will be welcome on Tours that LIV tried to undermine.

A spokesman for the DP World Tour said: “Given the high volume of inbound interest and enquiries, we are exploring the terms on which we are willing to accommodate players, provided they are free from third-party contractual restrictions and are willing to abide by our membership regulations. Our tournament committee has approved the process we intend to follow and we expect further enquiries in the days ahead.”

It sounds as though the DP World Tour might be more forgiving than the PGA Tour. Fair enough. But the prodigal LIV sons must be made to pay their dues, pay their fines, and go through a rigorous re-qualification process.

Article continues below

It should not be an easy reintegration. No way. But if it means a more compelling global game, it will be worth it.

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel should break unwritten rule for inspirational West Ham captain Jarrod Bowen
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel should break unwritten rule for inspirational West Ham captain Jarrod Bowen

Jarrod Bowen stayed with the Hammers despite their relegation to the Championship and has helped his side move to the top of the table after the opening six games of the season

View 3 Images Jarrod Bowen is leading West Ham by example in the Championship (Image: West Ham United FC/West Ham United FC via Getty Images)

It has become accepted football wisdom that Championship players should not make the England grade. Goalkeepers might have an outside chance because of a small pool of number ones in the Premier League, but not outfield players.

‌



The last Championship footballer to play a match for England was Sam Johnstone, who was West Bromwich Albion’s keeper when he earned three England caps in 2021. James Trafford earned a call-up from Thomas Tuchel when playing for Burnley in the Championship but did not make his debut until he was on Manchester City’s books.

‌



Since he became England manager, it is unlikely Tuchel has been to a Championship match. But he does not need to go to a match to make an exception to the Championship rule when he names his latest squad next week.

‌



He is unlikely to do it, but Tuchel should include Jarrod Bowen. And not just because his form has been predictably good for West Ham, not just because he scored a couple in the 3-2 win at Bolton the other night.

But because he bucked a trend. Because he showed qualities that are important in a character representing his country. Loyalty, spirit.

Bowen has suddenly not become below international class because he has played his last six matches in the Championship. He was very unlucky not to make Tuchel’s squad for the World Cup, don’t forget.

‌



Bowen has not stayed at West Ham purely out of love. He is extremely well-remunerated and perhaps there was not as much elite interest in him as might have been expected before he made his decision to remain at the club.

View 3 Images Thomas Tuchel will name his latest England squad next week (Image: Getty Images)

And it is a calculated gamble. Bowen might have realised this could be a thoroughly enjoyable season.

‌



He might have realised that being relegated from the Premier League does not need to be the doomsday scenario that so many like to imagine. West Ham fans might already be having more fun than they had in the entirety of last season.

They will see more goals - West Ham are averaging 2.3 a game as opposed to 1.2 a game last season - and they will see more wins. They will enjoy going to places such as Bolton. It makes a change. They will revel in the challenge of returning to the top flight.

View 3 Images Thomas Tuchel left Jarrod Bowen out of his World Cup squad (Image: Getty Images)

‌



They will see their team have the ball a lot more than they did last season. And they will not have to put up with the royal pain that VAR has become.

There is not a massive amount not to like. And, in their massive numbers, they will have a fantastic bond with a player who - after six and a half years at the club - has become one of their own.

Tuchel should not be in the business of handing out rewards to players just because they are nice guys. But Bowen is a very good player who is taking on a different challenge. And that should not mean his England career is put on hold.

Sports.title: Erling Haaland accuses Porto star of 'grabbing bottom' after angry bust-up on pitch
Sports.content:
Erling Haaland accuses Porto star of 'grabbing bottom' after angry bust-up on pitch

Erling Haaland was the Manchester City hero again in their Champions League victory over FC Porto, with the Norwegian striker notching both goals at the Estadio do Dragao

View 2 Images Erling Haaland clashes with Pablo Rosario (Image: Clive Brunskill)

Erling Haaland has claimed Pablo Rosario 'grabbed his bottom' as the two wrestled during Manchester City's fiery clash with Porto in the Champions League.

‌



Haaland scored twice in Portugal to give City a victory in their opening fixture, which was bad-tempered throughout. The Norway international and Rosario were both cautioned for a clash on the pitch, while there was also a confrontation between players and staff in the tunnel at half-time.

‌



Opening up on his tussle with Rosario, Haaland claimed the defender ended up grabbing his bottom during an interview with Norwegian television.

‌



“I was really keen on a hat-trick and it seemed like he [Rosario] was very eager to stop me from getting it. It was a little interesting, that. You’ll be seeing a picture where he’s grabbing my bottom... it’ll be interesting to see that picture,” he said.

Haaland, whose brace means he is now City's joint all-time top scorer in the Champions League with Sergio Aguero on 36 goals, admitted that Rosario and his Porto team-mates gave Enzo Maresca's side a real game.

‌



The Porto goalkeeper, Diogo Costa, had kept the Portuguese giants in the game with a string of fine saves in the first half before Haaland stuck. The 26-year-old broke the deadlock just two minutes after the restart before killing off any chance of the hosts snatching a share of the spoils with a 91st minute clincher.

“It was a difficult fight, man against man. They are a top team. Honestly, they are impressive,” he told Amazon Prime post-match.

View 2 Images Haaland scored both goals in Manchester City's 2-0 win over FC Porto (Image: Clive Brunskill/Getty Images)

‌



“I think honestly we controlled the first half. A bit uncomfortable when they came a bit high, but we created a lot of chances. I could easily have had a lot more goals, but second half we scored, and they pushed us for a good 25 minutes, but again we managed to hold through and then finish the game.

“I think these are the games that we have to win, and we have had a great start to the season. In the Champions League you have to win games because, if not, you suddenly get all the pressure, and then you never know what's going to happen.”

Sports.title: Jurgen Klopp in Trent Alexander-Arnold agreement with Jose Mourinho as boss issues verdict
Sports.content:
Jurgen Klopp in Trent Alexander-Arnold agreement with Jose Mourinho as boss issues verdict

Trent Alexander-Arnold has forced Real Madrid boss Jose Mourinho to reach a verdict - and it's a sentiment long echoed by Liverpool manager Jurgen Klopp

View 3 Images Trent Alexander-Arnold's performance in midfield for Real Madrid has made up Jose Mourinho's mind (Image: Getty)

Trent Alexander-Arnold was trialled in midfield by Real Madrid boss Jose Mourinho on Tuesday evening. But the Portuguese manager has reached the same conclusion as former Liverpool manager Jurgen Klopp: Alexander-Arnold is better as a right-back.

‌



Since moving to the Bernabeu last summer, the English defender has struggled with injuries. He did, however, make 35 appearances last term, registering five assists. Alas, with Mourinho's arrival came more roadblocks, as the ex-Chelsea, Manchester United and Tottenham boss sanctioned the signing of a new right-back.

‌



Netherlands international Denzel Dumfries has arrived from Inter Milan for £17million. In pre-season, Mourinho tried to play Alexander-Arnold alongside his new team-mate. In the Champions League on Tuesday evening, Inter Milan witnessed a brand new experiment.

‌



With Dumfries selected in defence to face his old club, former Liverpool vice-captain Alexander-Arnold was deployed in midfield. He had previously filled that role under Gareth Southgate for England, but this latest trial proved relatively ineffective despite the Spanish giants claiming a 2-1 victory.

Alexander-Arnold featured for 79 minutes before making way for Aurelien Tchouameni , and Mourinho has reached the same conclusion as Klopp: Alexander-Arnold is firmly a right-back, not a midfielder.

‌



His deployment in midfield was partially driven by Real Madrid's shortage of options in the centre of the pitch. Eduardo Camavinga, Arda Guler and Bernardo Silva were all unavailable due to UEFA carry-over suspensions.

Whilst Mourinho praised the player, he made a significant admission: "He has played midfield with England and Liverpool... But he is not a midfielder.

"He has played very well. He has interpreted what he needed to really well, tactically. Both him and [Federico] Valverde have worked very well at this level."

In 2023, during a Premier League fixture against Fulham, Alexander-Arnold, who had been operating as an inverted full-back, moved into a holding midfield position for the closing 30 minutes of the match. Liverpool secured a 4-3 victory with Alexander-Arnold netting an 88th-minute winner.

‌



However, ex-Reds boss Klopp made it abundantly clear after the final whistle that he did not consider the player a long-term midfield solution. He said: "I'm not stubborn and don't want to play him midfield, not at all, but I am not part of the discussion. You can discuss it as much as you want, but it will not have any influence.

View 3 Images Klopp never considered Trent Alexander-Arnold a midfielder (Image: Getty)

"Yes, Trent can play midfield but we always knew that Trent can play the role we gave him now very well as well. He became one of the most successful players in the history of Liverpool, in the recent history, playing as a right-back. He became a Premier League player as a right-back."

Two years before this, Klopp verbally reached the exact same conclusion as Mourinho has this week. In 2021, England manager Southgate chose to deploy Alexander-Arnold centrally rather than in his usual right-back position during a World Cup qualifier against Andorra.

He managed just 45 minutes there before being switched back to full-back. Klopp was baffled by the decision and told Sky Sports: "Why would you make the best right-back in the world a midfielder? I don't understand that really."

Sports.title: Trent Alexander-Arnold and Curtis Jones destroyed by foreign media after Liverpool reunion
Sports.content:
Trent Alexander-Arnold and Curtis Jones destroyed by foreign media after Liverpool reunion

Trent Alexander-Arnold and Curtis Jones were on opposite sides in the Champions League as Real Madrid beat Inter Milan, but both ex-Liverpool stars were lambasted

View 3 Images Trent Alexander-Arnold reunited with ex-Liverpool team-mate Curtis Jones in the Champions League (Image: SERGIO PEREZ/EPA/Shutterstock)

Spanish and Italian media tore into Trent Alexander-Arnold and Curtis Jones after the two ex-Liverpool stars reunited in the Champions League. Alexander-Arnold's Real Madrid beat Jones' new side Inter Milan 2-1 on Tuesday evening.

‌



The pair were born less than five miles apart and Alexander-Arnold joined the Reds' academy aged six, while Jones signed at nine. Both climbed up the ranks into the first team and became part of the squad that won multiple trophies in the following years.

‌



However, Alexander-Arnold departed for Real Madrid on a free transfer in the summer of 2025 and Jones waved goodbye to his boyhood club last month, signing for Inter Milan in a £30million deal.

‌



On Tuesday evening, Alexander-Arnold, positioned in midfield, came up against Jones, but media from Spain and Italy were far from impressed with either player.

‌



The Football Italia website savagely characterised the incident as a "brain f***" while Spanish publication AS accused Jones of "falling asleep" as he surrendered the ball.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."
