World.title: Betel nut traces in 25,000-year-old teeth point to early human drug use
World.content:
Betel nut, one of the most commonly used drugs in the world, appears to have an ancient history.

Fossilised remains of two people, found by archaeologists on the island of Sulawesi in Indonesia, carry traces of the psychoactive substance in their jaws.

One of the fossils is dated between 16,000 and 25,000 years old, making it the oldest known example of human drug use by at least 3,000 years.

The discovery was published today in the journal Science Advances.

The fossils belonged to human hunter-gatherers, both older than about 35. (Supplied: Fakhri)

Adam Brumm, lead author of the study and an archaeologist at Griffith University, said the two people probably sucked on betel nuts like "gobstoppers".

Professor Brumm, who tried the method himself, said it had a numbing effect on the mouth.

"I suspect that was the effect that they were after," he said.

Mysterious damaged teeth in Sulawesi caves

The fossils were uncovered by a team of Indonesian and Australian archaeologists at two separate sites in South Sulawesi.

Both individuals, the younger of which was 6,300 to 7,600 years old, predate the arrival of agriculture on Sulawesi.

Both hunter-gatherers had puzzling, deep marks on their teeth.

"Although they were separated by about 10,000 years of time, they had these really distinctive and very unusual tooth grooves," Professor Brumm said.

" We couldn't explain them. "

Damage to the teeth likely indicated a "lifelong habit", according to Adam Brumm. (Supplied: Mapang Project)

An analysis of the marks suggested they had been created by repeatedly sucking on a round object, one or two centimetres in size.

"I thought, immediately, betel nut is the most likely possibility," Professor Brumm said.

Betel nut by another method

Betel or areca nut is the seed of a palm native to South-East Asia.

It is one of the most commonly used psychoactive substances in the world, alongside alcohol, caffeine and nicotine.

Today, people typically grind betel nut and mix it with substances such as slaked lime to enhance its psychoactive properties before chewing it.

Betel nut is actually a seed from the fruit of the areca palm. (Supplied: Adam Brumm)

"We hypothesised that prior to the development of the betel nut chewing custom, there may have been an earlier stage in the human use of betel nut where they just sucked on the nut itself," Professor Brumm said.

To test this, the team designed an experiment to simulate betel nut sucking.

They soaked betel nuts in artificial saliva, then tested the saliva on frog egg cells, which had been genetically engineered to grow human brain receptors.

The results suggested betel nut sucking would affect human brain cells.

"It will alter human brain function, but not to the extent of modern betel nut chewing with slaked lime," Professor Brumm said.

Arecoline, the main psychoactive ingredient in betel nut, is similar to nicotine. (Supplied: Adam Brumm)

The team then investigated residues on the fossil teeth, finding arecoline, the main psychoactive substance in betel nut.

Sofia Samper Carro, an archaeologist at the Australian National University who was not involved in the research, agreed with the conclusion that betel nut sucking caused the tooth marks.

"The early evidence of drug consumption presented here predates any published evidence by thousands of years," Dr Samper Carro said.

Previously, the oldest known evidence of drug use was 13,000-year-old beer brewing in Israel.

A painful, addictive treatment

The researchers believe betel nut sucking would have produced a numbing effect on the mouth, and may have been used as a painkiller.

But betel nuts would have damaged teeth in the process, producing deep grooves that would have prompted painful toothaches.

Some grooves in the teeth stretched into the tooth pulp, likely causing toothaches. (Supplied: Mapang project)

Professor Brumm suggested the damaged teeth were evidence of a "vicious cycle".

"The more they sucked the nut for pain relief, the worse it damaged their teeth and the more they became addicted to sucking the nut to treat that."

Modern-day betel nut use also affects the mouth and teeth, and has been linked to an increased risk of oral cancer.

"You can see the pretty serious negative health consequences and how humans have grappled with those for at least 25,000 years on this island," Professor Brumm said.

Human fossils are rare in Sulawesi because of the humid climate. (Supplied: Basran Burhan)

Dr Samper Carro said the research could help identify even older uses of betel nut or other drugs.

"I'm convinced that even earlier hominids, such as Neanderthals, would have used natural remedies [like plants, natural compounds and maybe even insects or fungi] to fight pain and infection," she said.

Professor Brumm agreed the practice probably stretched further back into history than their 25,000-year-old sample.

"There's no human society today that doesn't use drugs of some kind," he said.

"But we just know so little about the deep antiquity of these practices."

World.title: Airlines call for air traffic control boss to quit over UK airport chaos
World.content:
The UK government has given National Air Traffic Services (NATS) one week to investigate the system failure that caused widespread flight cancellations at UK airports, with the company ruling out a cyber attack.

At least 2,000 flights were cancelled due to a fault in the flight data processing system operated by NATS on Tuesday, according to aviation analytics company Ciriumwith.

While the fault was fixed by Wednesdays, delays, cancellations and major disruption at UK airports continued with airlines reporting millions of pounds worth of financial loss.

Tens of thousands of passengers have been impacted after a technical issue grounded flights across the UK on Tuesday. (Reuters: Isabel Infantes)

The outage was the second major NATS failure in three years, prompting Britain's Transport minister Heidi Alexander to summon NATS CEO Martin Rolfe to explain what went wrong.

She later told parliament that she did "not believe this issue was unavoidable".

"I am clear that passengers should not have to face this disruption, I have therefore asked the [Civil Aviation Authority] to conduct an independent review to establish cause and ensure that our air traffic control systems can get passengers to where they need to be," she said.

The chief executive officer of budget airline Ryanair Michael O'Leary has called for Mr Rolfe to step down from the role, saying the outage was "an absolute re-run" of what happened in 2023.

Australians sleep at Heathrow after UK air traffic control failure Australian travellers have been left stranded at one of the world's busiest airports after an air traffic control failure led to flight cancellations across the United Kingdom.

Ryanair said its losses from Tuesday's outage were at least 3 million British pounds ($5.6 million), after the airline cancelled 260 flights affecting 48,000 passengers.

British Airways said it had had cancelled nearly 200 flights since the outage.

But a spokesperson for NATS said it was not the same issue as three years ago, and instead affected the flight data system.

"We will conduct a full investigation to establish the root cause and identify any further action required," the spokesperson said.

Mr Rolfe said his company had "at this point ruled out cyber" activity as a cause.

"We don't believe it was a cyberattack," he told the BBC.

"Our job is also to make sure that people stay safe.

"We never do this lightly. We only ever do it when there is an issue that cannot be resolved quickly, and we have to take action to make (sure) those who are flying, who are in the air at that time, are safe."

2023 shutdown caused $188 million in losses

NATS is a public-private partnership which is partially owned by airlines including British Airways and easyJet, pension funds and the government.

The last NATS shutdown in August 2023 caused travel chaos, costing airlines 100 million British pounds ($188 million).

That fault was caused when a flight plan containing a rare data conflict of two identically named waypoint markers caused systems to enter fail-safe mode. The shutdown lasted three hours until an engineer made it into work.

There was also a radar-related technical issue in July last year, which affected major airports including one of the world's biggest, Heathrow.

Ryanair is suing NATS at London's High Court, seeking more than 7 million British pounds ($13 million) over the 2023 outage.

It has called on NATS to reinvest its profits into performance improvements and hiring more staff.

The air traffic control provider paid its owners dividends of 175 million British Pounds ($328.5 million) in 2025.

Reuters

World.title: British police to investigate Reform UK after undercover documentary
World.content:
British police say they will carry out a criminal investigation into the populist Reform UK party following allegations made in a documentary that officials planned to break electoral law on foreign funding.

Reform, led by veteran Brexit campaigner Nigel Farage, denied any wrongdoing and a spokesman for the party said it would "fully cooperate" with the investigation.

London's Metropolitan Police said in a statement its detectives had assessed a number of "reports relating to donations and polling involving a political party" and had decided "there are potential offences requiring investigation".

"The potential offences are similar in nature to matters already under investigation by the Met's Special Enquiry Team relating to donations made to the same political party. As a result, these matters will form part of that ongoing investigation."

Hours before widening the investigation, the police announced they were going to be investigating allegations of breached donation rules.

Reform UK party leader and MP for Clacton, Nigel Farage, was captured on camera as part of a sting into donations to the party. (Reuters: Temilade Adelaja)

Documentary alleges electoral law breaches

The undercover investigation, broadcast by Channel 4 during Reform's annual conference, was conducted by investigative group Verbatim, which said it spent a year speaking to officials in Reform about possible donations.

It made several allegations including that the party had broken electoral law by arranging for a foreign donor to pay for political polling.

It showed two senior officials in Reform — then head of policy James Orr and Mr Farage's former right-hand man, Dan Jukes — speaking about funding with a supposed US businessman and his British-based son, including conversations about a payment for three opinion polls commissioned by the party.

Posing as wealthy donors from the United States with British connections, the undercover reporters eventually had a lunch with Mr Farage who later told the BBC he was not listening to what was said.

Mr Farage, under investigation by a parliamentary watchdog about earlier donations, was forced to sack the close senior aides last week after the documentary aired.

On Friday, Reform launched an internal investigation and denied the allegations, saying the party had been the victim of a hoax perpetrated by climate activists.

Mr Farage described some of the comments as little more than "loose pub talk".

Farage defiant as Reform aides step down over foreign donations sting Dan Jukes, the leader's senior aide, and James Orr, the party’s head of policy, have stepped down from their roles while the party conducts an internal investigation.

The widening of the criminal investigation piles pressure on Reform, whose commanding lead in opinion polls has faltered over other allegations, including a 5 million British pounds ($9.3 million) gift to Mr Farage, focus of the parliamentary probe.

Reform's annual conference last week, when Mr Farage wanted to set a vision for Reform's first 100 days in power if it wins the next national election, was overshadowed by the undercover investigation.

Instead of talking about a national election, which must be held by mid-2029 at the latest, Reform spent almost equal amounts of time either vigorously denying the accusations or trying to ignore them.

"We won't be commenting further while a live investigation is underway," the Reform spokesman said.

Reuters

World.title: Three Lindsay Clancy jurors raise concerns after mistrial
World.content:
Three members of the Lindsay Clancy jury have spoken about failing to reach a consensus in an interview with US media.

Warning: This story contains details of a crime that may be distressing for some readers.

Foreperson Roni Carlson said all but one member of the jury were persuaded to find the defendant not guilty by reason of insanity, in an interview with NBC10 Boston.

After deliberating, Ms Carlson described being "excited" the jury had reached a consensus.

She began filling out the paperwork, but was interrupted by the lone juror.

"He had reasonable doubt, he admitted he had reasonable doubt," she said.

"But he said 'I'm still not gonna say she's not guilty by reason of insanity'."

Lindsay Clancy was charged with three counts of first-degree murder over the deaths of her three children at their Boston home on January 24, 2023.

The Massachusetts mother's attorney said she had lost control of her mind due to postpartum psychosis, while prosecutors argued she knew what she was doing and acted deliberately.

After six-weeks of testimony, the judge ultimately declared a mistrial when the jury could not come to an agreement.

Loading Instagram content

Proof beyond a reasonable doubt?

The three jurors interviewed, Roni Carlson, Kellie Farina and Paula Devlin, raised concerns the lone juror's doubt did not match his verdict.

In the United States, the Due Process Clause in the constitution "requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt before a person may be convicted of a crime".

Judge William Sullivan addresses the jury during deliberations. (AP: Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via Pool)

Ms Devlin described the lone juror as "very arrogant".

"He really did not take on anything that anybody said," she said.

She continued to describe an interaction where he asked jury members who are nurses about Ms Clancy's medication and the toxicology report.

But then, Ms Devlin said, "he just completely disregarded the information that they gave".

'Did she know right from wrong?'

Ms Carlson explained that the majority found Ms Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity due to the evidence presented regarding her character and mental health.

"We weren't trying to figure out if she murdered the children, she did and she's admitting that," she said.

"We're trying to figure out did she know right from wrong at that time.

"Everything proved she loved her children — from her journals to her mother-in-law — everything proved that she loved her children so she had to have snapped and not know what she was doing."

The three women left the six-week trial as life-long friends, according to NBC10 Boston, saying they supported each other through the traumatic testimony.

Ms Farina described hearing Patrick Clancy's, Lindsay's husband, 911 call.

"It's something I will never not hear," Ms Farina said.

"When we heard it again in the jury room we were crying again, we were just like 'my god, the desperation, the despair in his voice'.

What happens next in Lindsay Clancy case The six-week criminal trial of Lindsay Clancy has collapsed without a verdict, with the judge declaring a mistrial.

"I felt that it was genuine."

Although the trial ended without a verdict, the case is not closed and prosecutors are free to start a new trial with a new jury.

Plymouth County District Attorney Tim Cruz told reporters that no decision had been made on whether prosecutors would retry the case, but that his goal was always "getting justice for those three little babies".

World.title: Veterans headstone project fears funding promise falls short of need
World.content:
An organisation that helps to locate and name veterans in unmarked graves in South Australia is raising concerns about whether promised federal funding will be delivered.

The Headstone Project locates World War I veterans in unmarked graves and places a military service headstone there to recognise their service to Australia.

President of the SA branch, John Brownlie, said giving a veteran a headstone cost about $1,500 and that federal government grants contributed $620 toward that cost.

Getting a headstone for this veteran's grave will cost about $1,500. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

Before the 2022 federal election, Labor committed $3.7 million in funding for the Headstone Project nationally.

Federal budget papers show $1.4 million over five years from 2025-2026 has been allocated for a range of memorial initiatives, including the Marking (First World War) Private Graves Grants program, which is the grant the Headstone Project applies for.

Those grant guidelines, as seen by the ABC, show only $58,000 is available nationally for this financial year.

The Headstone Project SA believes that number to be below what should be available.

These two nurses were given headstones that recognised their service. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

Mr Brownlie queried the amount.

"Look at what you've [the federal government] promised, and look at what you've delivered, because there's a vast discrepancy," Mr Brownlie said.

"I think the behaviour of the government, quite frankly, is egregious."

The federal government did not provide an on-the-record response to the concerns raised by the Headstone Project SA, but the ABC understands all eligible applications have been awarded grant funding.

Deserve recognition

Ian Hopley is a former police officer who now investigates unmarked graves to provide military headstones. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

Ian Hopley is a retired police officer who now assists with finding graves, determining that a veteran is buried in the grave and then researching and contacting living relatives.

The team searches cemetery records and picks out males of enlistment age born between 1870 and 1900; they then cross-check that with the national archives and find the graves of forgotten veterans.

Mr Hopley said the SA branch had provided headstones to nearly 200 servicemen and women and that about 500 were known around the state still to be waiting.

"Our work will go on for a very long time, provided we get the right funding and support," he said.

Mr Hopley said he came from a military family and believed the people in unmarked graves should be recognised for their service.

World.title: 'Wrong decision': New babies' hospital plans slammed by doctors
World.content:
Plans to manage high-risk births at WA's new Women and Babies Hospital represent the government doubling down on a "wrong decision", the doctors' lobby says.

The hospital is being built next to Fiona Stanley Hospital in Murdoch, about 20 kilometres from Perth Children's Hospital (PCH) where some infants will need to be transferred for specialist care.

Doctors and parents have long said the distance is unacceptable and called on the government to find a way of building the hospital on the QEII campus in Nedlands to make it easier for women and babies to be transferred to PCH and Sir Charles Gairdner Hospital.

Doctors say the new hospital, which is currently under construction, is too far from existing facilities. (ABC News: Courtney Withers )

But the government maintains that is impossible without unacceptable disruption to other hospitals on the site, or intolerable delays.

Instead, the government has now outlined how it intends to allay the concerns of medical professionals and families by expanding existing services.

Neonate transfer upgrade

Paediatric services at Fiona Stanley Hospital will be upgraded, including extra specialist staff and services, and a second Newborn Emergency Transport Service (NETS) base established for babies who need to be transferred from the new hospital.

New $1.8b maternity hospital to be built at Fiona Stanley The WA premier announces plans to build a maternity hospital at the Queen Elizabeth II Medical Centre will no longer go ahead, instead committing almost $2b to a site in Perth's south.

"We've heard from clinicians that the time for the baby to reach the NETS team is a key consideration," Health Minister Meredith Hammat said.

"These are specialised staff, these are like mobile intensive care units and so they do provide that critical opportunity to stabilise a baby and transport them, so that is why we're making the decision about having a base here."

The government also believes locating a team at Murdoch will help with the timely transfer of babies from regional hospitals, because it is closer to Jandakot Airport where Royal Flying Doctor Service aircraft land.

Meredith Hammat says it is the right decision. (ABC News: Courtney Withers )

More beds

Around $95 million has been set aside to add an extra 19 beds to PCH's neonatal intensive care unit.

Two adult beds will be added to handle a "very small number of cases" where women needed to birth at the children's hospital.

A new high-risk birthing unit is due to be built at Perth Children's Hospital. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

A consultation report, dated November 2025 but only tabled in parliament today, revealed clinicians rejected the idea of creating a smaller "satellite" facility to allow for births at PCH "due to clinical safety risks, limited workforce sustainability and fragmentation of services".

Doctors issue warning over maternity hospital move Doctors fear plans to move WA's main women's and babies' hospital 20 kilometres from its current location risk increased "mortality and morbidity" of critically unwell infants.

Ms Hammat said few women would give birth at PCH.

"It would only apply in those circumstances, a small number of circumstances, where a parent might also need to continue to receive treatment," Ms Hammat said.

Ongoing concerns

Australian Medical Association WA president Kyle Hoath said while the government's announcements were welcome, the profession still wanted the new hospital to be built at the QEII site.

Doctors want the new hospital to be built at the QEII site. (ABC News: Gregor Salmon)

"I appreciate that it's a full site that's difficult to make those allowances on, but this isn't good enough," he said. "We have a separation of services that need to be next to each other."

Opposition Health spokesperson Libby Mettam also wants a maternity hospital at the QEII site and said the government's plans were "flawed".

"It will still require a 20-kilometre journey for neonates requiring high-risk surgery at Perth Children's Hospital," she said.

Work begins on Perth's new $1.8b maternity hospital Perth's new Women and Babies Hospital will open on time, the state government insists, but it says the $1.8 billion budget may blow out.

Dr Hoath said his members believed between 100 and 200 babies a year would need to be moved to PCH.

The government's response to the November 2025 consultation report notes there is "no consensus on the size of the cohort needing 'time-critical neonatal transfer'".

The upgrades at PCH will require admin staff to be moved out of the building and the relocation of a surgical ward.

World.title: Hollands opens up on axing from Carlton AFL roster
World.content:
Elijah Hollands is at peace with the end of his Carlton career, saying he realises there are more important things in life that he needs to focus on.

Hollands was one of seven players delisted by the Blues on Wednesday, with former GWS star Zac Williams, Jordan Boyd, Lachie Fogarty, Lewis Young, Flynn Young and Harry Charleson also among the casualties.

But it was Hollands' axing just months after suffering an on-field mental health episode that represented the biggest story.

Carlton was fined $75,000 for its handling of Hollands during a round-six loss to Collingwood.

Hollands tallied just one disposal for the match, with his erratic behaviour catching the attention of fans even before the game started.

The 24-year-old was hospitalised days later before deciding to step away from football to concentrate on his mental health.

It meant Hollands wasn't able to add to his 47-game AFL career, 14 of which were played at Gold Coast.

His brother Oliver Hollands remains at Carlton.

Elijah took to Instagram to share his thoughts about the end of his time at the Blues, which could also spell an end to his AFL career.

Loading Instagram content

"Football means an extreme amount to me," Hollands wrote.

"My dad played professional footy, my great-grandfather played professional footy, my brother plays professional footy — it is everything I have lived and breathed for as long as I can remember.

"I have only ever wanted to do one thing my entire life: copy what was done before me and play AFL footy. It was something that I just knew I was going to do when I was a kid and it was all I ever cared about.

"And now, unfortunately, that purpose I had is no longer.

"I love this game, but I have come to realise that there are things in my life that are far more important than footy right now and they're the things I will now prioritise."

Hollands's father posts heartfelt message Elijah Hollands's father, former AFL player Ben Hollands, posts on social media pledging to help lift his son up and urging others to check on their friends if they are struggling.

Hollands thanked the greater AFL community for its support since his mental health challenges became public.

"As an extremely confident 18-year-old, I certainly envisioned my career going a whole lot differently, but I am OK with accepting that it just isn't in the plans set for me," Hollands said.

"I'll be moving into the next chapter of my life, leaving what will feel like a big hole to fill, but I am excited about what can come from having my health and mind in much greater shape."

Carlton's other big delisting was Williams, who joined the Blues from GWS at the end of 2020 on a six-year deal believed to be worth about $5 million.

The soon-to-be 32-year-old managed only nine games this year, with his time at Carlton plagued by injuries.

AAP

World.title: Anthropic researcher says some developers believe AI 'could kill us all'
World.content:
Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon has quit the AI company, saying those building the technology "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade".

Mr Coxon said he had spent the past three years doing pre-training research at Anthropic and OpenAI.

"Neither company is acting responsibly," he posted on X.

"They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."

Superintelligence is considered to be the stage of AI when machines surpass human performance in every field.

Anthropic Alignment Science lead Evan Hubinger posted a reply on X saying Mr Coxon was correct.

"We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10 per cent within the next decade," he wrote.

"I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to."

Mr Coxon is one of a growing number of AI experts to call on the industry to slow down.

In July more than 1,300 employees of frontier AI companies signed a statement saying there was a "real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems".

The letter called on the US government to support an international effort to develop tools that can "deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development".

CEO and co-founder of Anthropic, Dario Amodei. (Reuters: Denis Balibouse)

Responding to the initiative in July, called Pacing the Frontier, Anthropic said in an X post: "Our own research on recursive self-improvement, published last month, points to the need for tools to deliberately pace the frontier of AI development ⁠so society can prepare".

OpenAI also responded to the letter, posting on X at the time: "We believe that, at some point in the future, AI acceleration ‌for ⁠frontier model development may be so high that the world will need to pace the rate of AI advancement."

AI could pose 'existential' risk, UN warns

The "alignment problem" for superintelligence is that an AI system may not share human values.

Autonomous drones and AI called out by UN human rights chief UN-rights chief has addressed a council in Geneva saying AI posed a threat to humanity.

On Monday, United Nations rights chief Volker Turk also warned that artificial intelligence could pose a threat to humanity and pledged to press AI firms to reduce risks that his office said included disruptions to services, communications and democratic systems.

He called for "cast-iron guarantees" to secure AI in a speech ahead of the start of his unprecedented second term.

"I share the concerns of industry insiders that advanced AI could pose an existential risk to humanity," Mr Turk told the body in Geneva.

"I am calling here, today, for an all-out effort to put cast-iron guarantees in place around the safety and security of AI before it is too late."

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Boxing coach gunned down in latest Sydney gangland attack
World.content:
A boxing coach has been shot dead in an ambush in Sydney’s south-west, in what police believe is another targeted attack linked to organised crime. Louis Meehan, 32, was killed behind his boxing gym in the carpark of the Punchbowl Community Centre on Wednesday evening after being sprayed by gunfire by an assailant inside a silver Lexus sedan. Louis Meehan has been shot dead in the latest attack linked to Sydney’s gangland violence. Janie Barrett Police rushed to the carpark, administering urgent CPR to Meehan, while two onlookers knelt to pray for the man before he was pronounced dead. Meehan was walking alone when he was shot beside a white sedan at the entry of the carpark, which was full at the time of the attack.



Onlookers, including multiple school students, watched on from the edge of the carpark as paramedics worked to save him. Meehan has posed online wearing merchandise linked to the Alameddine crime gang. This includes clothing from Proper 60, a Merrylands-based group associated with the family, and Ready 4 War, the name of the Alameddine network’s drug-trafficking operation. Meehan was killed near the entry to the carpark. Janie Barrett Campsie Police Area Commander Dean Johnstone confirmed Meehan was known to police. “This is a callous act,” he said. “We do not believe that other persons were at risk. However, obviously, in a public place like this, those actions cannot be tolerated.”



Police had no information to suggest that Meehan’s life was in immediate danger, or an underworld contract had been taken out for his murder, according to Johnstone. Meehan, the son of former Australian boxing great Kali Meehan, played for the Sydney Roosters’ National Youth Competition side alongside brother Willis in 2013 before turning to full-time boxing coaching. Desperate paramedics attempted to save Meehan. SCN WorldStar He was a senior coach on the ‘Meehan Boxing Team’, a family-run business that conducted personal training sessions and boxing classes. His brothers are also involved in the business. The Punchbowl Community Centre carpark sits one block behind The Boulevarde, a busy high street adjacent to Punchbowl train station.



It is on the same road as St Jerome’s Catholic Primary School and St Jerome’s Catholic Church. The street has been roped off and blocked by marked and unmarked cars. Police have expanded the crime scene as they work to gather evidence. An expanded crime scene has been set up outside the community centre in Punchbowl. Janie Barrett The Punchbowl shooting comes two days after the Minns government announced a suite of measures targeting an outbreak of gangland violence on Sydney’s streets. The measures were flagged in response to last week’s mistaken identity killings of university student Marco Tapia, 23, and business owner Joshua Macdonald, 40, in the city’s west.



The reforms promised tighter targeting of offshore kingpins and local middle men orchestrating violent attacks and tougher penalties for teenagers carrying out gang-related shootings and firebombings. It marked the NSW government’s third significant crackdown on organised crime in two years and came days after the police minister denied authorities had lost control of escalating violence. Loading Conflict between the Alameddine crime family and Coconut Cartel has sparked an escalation in underworld violence in recent years, as the warring organised crime syndicates jostle for control of Sydney’s lucrative drug trade. Powerbrokers for both of the groups are living overseas, where they’re believed to be orchestrating criminal activities in Sydney while out of reach of Australian police.



Asked on Monday if community fears were justified following last week’s shootings, Premier Chris Minns said: “We do think there’s a problem.” “There [is] a disregard for human life I haven’t really seen before,” he said. “It’s been a regrettable and horrible part of life in Sydney.” It followed Police Minister Yasmin Catley’s insistence last week that the violence was not “out of control”. Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane referenced Catley’s comments following the Punchbowl shooting on Wednesday, writing on X: “Another deadly shooting in Sydney – the 3rd in a week. This time in front of a community centre. Do you still have things under control police minister Catley?”



Innocent men Marco Tapia, 23, and Joshua Macdonald were killed a day apart last week in what police say were cases of mistaken identity. Tapia was killed last Tuesday morning after a group of home invaders stormed his family’s Glen Alpine home before executing him in his bed. He was in his third year of a biomedical engineering degree at the University of Technology Sydney, and his only brush with the law was through a minor traffic offence. Macdonald was shot dead in the doorway of a Merrylands West duplex home the next day. CCTV footage outside the home showed a grey Audi sedan stopping outside the house before an assassin fires shots from the back passenger seat.



Macdonald, who didn’t live at the home, was arriving at the duplex with a resident and two children moments before he was shot. The owners of the Bruce Street residence are known to police and linked to organised crime. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: It was the most stressful thing she’s ever done, but the Traitors winner would do it all again
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On Wednesday night, Kirby Bentley was named winner of the rebooted The Traitors Australia, claiming a prize pot of $200,600. The former Australian Survivor contestant and AFLW player was an OG Traitor who manoeuvred her way through the reality competition as her fellow Traitors – former Bachelor contestant Alex Nation, former MasterChef Australia contestant Alvin Quah and comedian Rhys Nicholson – were picked off by the Faithfuls. Called a “parlour game sociopath” in the final episode, Kirby had to convince The Real Housewives of Sydney’s Krissy Marsh and former Bachelor contestant Keira Maguire at the fire pit that she was a Faithful. Spoiler alert: She was not! Bentley talks to national TV editor Louise Rugendyke about her victory, what makes her such a good manipulator and which competition was harder: Australian Survivor or The Traitors? The Traitors Australia winner Kirby Bentley and host Gretel Killeen. Hello Kirby! How are you feeling now that it’s all over? It looked very stressful. It’s been an incredible experience. The show is just so complex that when you’re watching it, you’re like, “That’s that’s so simple, and it’s so obvious”, but it genuinely isn’t. I’m really relieved [it’s over] because it’s a stressful game. It was a wild ride, and they’ve done an incredible job [with the edit]. The show was filmed at an historic estate, Castle Claremont, in New Zealand’s South Island. How long did the shoot take? It was 12 days of filming, and I think 12 days is the maximum that I probably could have lasted because the moral dilemma of the human in you starts to play a part, and I was a Traitor the whole time. And it’s not a comfortable position to be in, when everyone’s their authentic self as faithfuls – and we’ve all got trust issues – so it’s just a really bizarre experience.



Related Article Spoliers

Reality TV What’s next for the winner of Alone Australia? He’s writing a cookbook, obviously What were you thinking on that first night, when host Gretel Killeen was choosing the Traitors, and you felt her hand on your shoulder? I genuinely wasn’t expecting it. I think I said to Gretel when she had asked if I wanted to be a Traitor, I was like, “If I’m a Traitor, I get to play the game and move the game the way that I need to as a Survivor person”, because there’s a reputation - “Survivor this, Survivor that” – that it has to be one of us [picked as a Traitor]. And I was like, “No, it doesn’t.” So when she selected me, I was so excited because if I wasn’t [picked], I would have been gone pretty early. How much did being a former Survivor player affect the way you played, especially when you had so much heat on you early on? The cast of Traitors Australia, which was made up of former reality stars. In an ideal circumstance, where you don’t wear clothes that Kween Kong can hear [Kween said she could hear the rustle of Kirby’s jacket when Gretel tapped her on the shoulder], I would have liked to have played a little bit lower. Let’s just bite the bullet and get Kween gone, and we’ll deal with the repercussions the next day.” There’s so much paranoia around Faithfuls, but it worked out a lot easier than I thought it was going to. I play a really aggressive game in Survivor, and it’s really cutthroat. If anyone ever says my name, it’s “Let’s just get them gone” and create that fear. And I did the same in this, and it worked. OK, Kirby, what is it about you that makes you so cutthroat? Why do you keep getting cast in these shows? I mean, you seem pretty nice to me.

World.title: Australian cars stolen for parts to sell to Iran and Russia, insurers say
World.content:
Exclusive BusinessConsumer affairsOrganised crime Australian cars stolen for parts to sell to Iran and Russia, insurers say Elias Visontay September 9, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Organised crime groups are stealing cars from Australian roads, shipping them overseas and stripping them down to sell the parts in Iran and Russia, insurers have warned, as sanctions make the black market for parts increasingly lucrative. The revelation from the Insurance Council of Australia comes amid fresh data showing Melbourne remains Australia’s vehicle theft epicentre. This is propelled by petty crime as well as organised syndicates packing stolen cars into shipping containers, sending them to intermediary ports to bypass detection before forwarding them to sanctioned nations. Stolen Australian cars are being shipped overseas, dismantled and sold to Iran and Russia where the black market for smuggled replacement components has become highly lucrative. Aresna Villanueva Victoria recorded over 12,300 car-theft claims in the 2025-26 financial year, costing insurers $244.3 million. While the number of theft claims remained stable, total costs grew by more than $21 million. More cars are stolen or broken into in Melbourne than in all other capital cities combined. Queensland motorists lodged 6200 theft claims costing $113 million, while there were roughly 5500 claims costing $98.7 million in NSW. In Western Australia, about 3500 claims cost $22 million. Nationally, the financial toll of car thefts exceeded half a billion dollars.



Insurance Council chief executive Andrew Hall said that while car theft includes joyriding and domestic re-selling, insurers believe a growing proportion of vehicles are stolen specifically for overseas export. Hall noted insurers report that two-thirds of vehicles stolen in Melbourne are never recovered locally and that detections of Australian-registered vehicle parts overseas have increased. Throughout the year, Victorian and Queensland police have raided shipping containers at Melbourne and Brisbane ports and at wrecking yards, uncovering hidden stolen vehicles. Authorities have also made a string of arrests linked to an international crime syndicate that has illegally shipped tens of millions of dollars worth of stolen cars to the United Arab Emirates. In an interview with this masthead, Hall revealed that insurers had since formed the belief that after arriving in the UAE on illegal shipments, the cars were being dismantled for parts to be sent primarily to Iran and Russia. A lucrative market for second-hand replacement components has emerged because sanctions prohibit manufacturers from selling legitimate parts to repairers in those countries.



Related Article Crime Hacked, stolen and shipped overseas: Police crack global car theft ring “Australia has become part of a global supply chain for sanctioned nations,” Hall said. While some crime groups have been busted by police, he said the broader problem was ongoing. “We’ve got examples of authorities overseas finding shipping containers of Victorian registered vehicles in the UAE,” he said. “We don’t check things that leave the country.” He noted that since local car manufacturing ended, any shipping container full of cars leaving Australia should raise suspicion. Discovering right-hand drive models (made for left side of road driving systems) at Australian ports destined for left-hand drive countries is a telltale sign that they are illegitimate shipments destined to be dismantled.



Common Japanese and Korean-manufactured brands are among the most targeted due to their prominence among Iranian and Russian motorists, Hall said. Australia’s relatively open supply chain, which similarly enabled an influx of illicit tobacco, is a key factor attracting organised criminals to car smuggling, Hall said. Syndicate leaders are hiring teenagers to steal cars because they can be paid less and face more lenient judicial consequences, Hall said. His comments echo concerns from NSW police that local crime groups are adopting European gang tactics, relying on teenage boys to take great risks for a fraction of adult costs. “It’s teenagers, they’ve got no consequences in their mind, and can earn $1000 stealing a car and delivering it to a drop-off point,” Hall said. “They might get arrested, but get bailed and do it again, bailed and do it again.” Modern cars with proximity keys that do not need to be put into the ignition have become easier targets. Thieves use specialist devices to amplify the signal from a key inside a house to unlock the car parked outside. This vulnerability has led to a rise in the use of manual steering wheel locks.

World.title: Boxing coach gunned down in latest Sydney gangland attack
World.content:
A boxing coach has been shot dead in an ambush in Sydney’s south-west, in what police believe is another targeted attack linked to organised crime. Louis Meehan, 32, was killed behind his boxing gym in the carpark of the Punchbowl Community Centre on Wednesday evening after being sprayed by gunfire by an assailant inside a silver Lexus sedan. Louis Meehan has been shot dead in the latest attack linked to Sydney’s gangland violence. Janie Barrett Police rushed to the carpark, administering urgent CPR to Meehan, while two onlookers knelt to pray for the man before he was pronounced dead. Meehan was walking alone when he was shot beside a white sedan at the entry of the carpark, which was full at the time of the attack.



Onlookers, including multiple school students, watched on from the edge of the carpark as paramedics worked to save him. Meehan has posed online wearing merchandise linked to the Alameddine crime gang. This includes clothing from Proper 60, a Merrylands-based group associated with the family, and Ready 4 War, the name of the Alameddine network’s drug-trafficking operation. Meehan was killed near the entry to the carpark. Janie Barrett Campsie Police Area Commander Dean Johnstone confirmed Meehan was known to police. “This is a callous act,” he said. “We do not believe that other persons were at risk. However, obviously, in a public place like this, those actions cannot be tolerated.”



Police had no information to suggest that Meehan’s life was in immediate danger, or an underworld contract had been taken out for his murder, according to Johnstone. Meehan, the son of former Australian boxing great Kali Meehan, played for the Sydney Roosters’ National Youth Competition side alongside brother Willis in 2013 before turning to full-time boxing coaching. Desperate paramedics attempted to save Meehan. SCN WorldStar He was a senior coach on the ‘Meehan Boxing Team’, a family-run business that conducted personal training sessions and boxing classes. His brothers are also involved in the business. The Punchbowl Community Centre carpark sits one block behind The Boulevarde, a busy high street adjacent to Punchbowl train station.



It is on the same road as St Jerome’s Catholic Primary School and St Jerome’s Catholic Church. The street has been roped off and blocked by marked and unmarked cars. Police have expanded the crime scene as they work to gather evidence. An expanded crime scene has been set up outside the community centre in Punchbowl. Janie Barrett The Punchbowl shooting comes two days after the Minns government announced a suite of measures targeting an outbreak of gangland violence on Sydney’s streets. The measures were flagged in response to last week’s mistaken identity killings of university student Marco Tapia, 23, and business owner Joshua Macdonald, 40, in the city’s west.



The reforms promised tighter targeting of offshore kingpins and local middle men orchestrating violent attacks and tougher penalties for teenagers carrying out gang-related shootings and firebombings. It marked the NSW government’s third significant crackdown on organised crime in two years and came days after the police minister denied authorities had lost control of escalating violence. Loading Conflict between the Alameddine crime family and Coconut Cartel has sparked an escalation in underworld violence in recent years, as the warring organised crime syndicates jostle for control of Sydney’s lucrative drug trade. Powerbrokers for both of the groups are living overseas, where they’re believed to be orchestrating criminal activities in Sydney while out of reach of Australian police.



Asked on Monday if community fears were justified following last week’s shootings, Premier Chris Minns said: “We do think there’s a problem.” “There [is] a disregard for human life I haven’t really seen before,” he said. “It’s been a regrettable and horrible part of life in Sydney.” It followed Police Minister Yasmin Catley’s insistence last week that the violence was not “out of control”. Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane referenced Catley’s comments following the Punchbowl shooting on Wednesday, writing on X: “Another deadly shooting in Sydney – the 3rd in a week. This time in front of a community centre. Do you still have things under control police minister Catley?”



Innocent men Marco Tapia, 23, and Joshua Macdonald were killed a day apart last week in what police say were cases of mistaken identity. Tapia was killed last Tuesday morning after a group of home invaders stormed his family’s Glen Alpine home before executing him in his bed. He was in his third year of a biomedical engineering degree at the University of Technology Sydney, and his only brush with the law was through a minor traffic offence. Macdonald was shot dead in the doorway of a Merrylands West duplex home the next day. CCTV footage outside the home showed a grey Audi sedan stopping outside the house before an assassin fires shots from the back passenger seat.



Macdonald, who didn’t live at the home, was arriving at the duplex with a resident and two children moments before he was shot. The owners of the Bruce Street residence are known to police and linked to organised crime. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

A lucrative market for second-hand replacement components has emerged because sanctions prohibit manufacturers from selling legitimate parts to repairers in those countries.



Related Article Crime Hacked, stolen and shipped overseas: Police crack global car theft ring “Australia has become part of a global supply chain for sanctioned nations,” Hall said. While some crime groups have been busted by police, he said the broader problem was ongoing. “We’ve got examples of authorities overseas finding shipping containers of Victorian registered vehicles in the UAE,” he said. “We don’t check things that leave the country.” He noted that since local car manufacturing ended, any shipping container full of cars leaving Australia should raise suspicion. Discovering right-hand drive models (made for left side of road driving systems) at Australian ports destined for left-hand drive countries is a telltale sign that they are illegitimate shipments destined to be dismantled.



Common Japanese and Korean-manufactured brands are among the most targeted due to their prominence among Iranian and Russian motorists, Hall said. Australia’s relatively open supply chain, which similarly enabled an influx of illicit tobacco, is a key factor attracting organised criminals to car smuggling, Hall said. Syndicate leaders are hiring teenagers to steal cars because they can be paid less and face more lenient judicial consequences, Hall said. His comments echo concerns from NSW police that local crime groups are adopting European gang tactics, relying on teenage boys to take great risks for a fraction of adult costs. “It’s teenagers, they’ve got no consequences in their mind, and can earn $1000 stealing a car and delivering it to a drop-off point,” Hall said. “They might get arrested, but get bailed and do it again, bailed and do it again.” Modern cars with proximity keys that do not need to be put into the ignition have become easier targets. Thieves use specialist devices to amplify the signal from a key inside a house to unlock the car parked outside. This vulnerability has led to a rise in the use of manual steering wheel locks.

World.title: Law change will address development contributions for out-of-sequence projects - minister
World.content:
The infrastructure minister says a law change is imminent that will address council concerns over development contributions for out-of-sequence projects.

It follows concerns from Auckland Council over unanticipated development, and the infrastructure bill the council faces.

The council has started an investigation into how to tell developers, and potential residents, that it will not provide or fund services.

Chris Bishop says the council has got ahead of itself, but has conceded there needs to be a better way to recover infrastructure costs for out-of-sequence growth.

Auckland councillors were told on Tuesday that Auckland faced a potential infrastructure bill of up to $5 billion, from the approval of 50,000 to 60,000 "unanticipated" homes, meaning homes being built outside of Auckland's planned growth areas and planning processes.

The chair of the council's planning committee, Richard Hills, told Morning Report on Wednesday the council had identified areas for future growth, but these homes were being proposed outside of those areas.

"There's compounding factors of constant approval of housing that we don't have plans for, we don't have infrastructure for, we don't have funding for, and what's broke the camel's back, I guess, is the fast-track," he said.

Fast-track housing could leave buyers without council services Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Hills said the council would not be able to build the required infrastructure, partly because of the anticipated rates caps.

"We have to draw the line. We have to make people know that if you're buying into those areas, we may not be able to fund it. We're going to prioritise you last because we have to somehow upgrade the infrastructure, and pay for services in the already really spread out Auckland that we all face today."

The council has commissioned some independent advice on its options, which Hills expected to present in October.

But the council has also asked staff to determine what its legal options are, including what the council could do around charging developers or residents more, or de-prioritising certain services.

"Those people will still pay some rates, but do we put them on a slightly lower rate that acknowledges you're in a fast-track area or an area of no service? Because, the developers are saying that the residents' associations will run the water supply and the wastewater. We know that if they fail, they'll come back to all of us to pay for in the end anyway.

"But overall, other services, like animal management, like noise control, like illegal dumping, to continue to keep spreading out these services, having people drive far further, is just an impossible task for us to do while trying to keep rates low."

Hills anticipated pushback from the government and from developers, and on Thursday Bishop said Hills was getting ahead of himself.

"If a fast-track project turns up that's out of sequence with what the council's got in its its plan, they'll be able to amend their development contributions, which are paid by developers for the growth charges for infrastructure, in order to recover the costs of that infrastructure."

Bishop said the government's core policy was that growth should pay for growth.

"If there's infrastructure required to service developments that are out of sequence, then the development contributions paid by developers should be able to make those costs, and that's a core government objective. That's always been our objective."

Bishop said the 50,000 to 60,000 number was over the next 20 to 30 years.

"Firstly, they've got to apply. Secondly, they've got to be approved, and then there'll be infrastructure conditions attached to all of that, and obviously development contributions to contribute towards that."

World.title: Dozens of academic papers have references made up by AI - research
World.content:
Dozens of academic papers have fake references in them that have been made up by AI, according to new research from the University of Auckland.

The study looked at more than 3000 peer-reviewed papers published in the last few years and found 2 percent of them - or 69 papers - had fake references hallucinated by AI.

Some of the references had realistic author and journal names and publication details - but when the researchers went looking for them, they did not exist.

In a research paper, each reference is meant to be a promise, that if anybody wanted to check the evidence a claim is based on, they could. But what happens if that reference does not lead anywhere?

University of Auckland computer science lecturer Ulrich Speidel was one of the co-authors of a research paper which looked at that problem.

"I can remember going through one, where out of I think 29 references in the paper there wasn't a single one that actually existed. When you look at them initially, they all look - pompous titles, real names for the articles, in some cases real journals."

They were published papers in fields related to AI in education that had gone through the peer review process and been checked by other academics.

Speidel said they found that online academic database Google Scholar had also fallen victim to the problem.

"If enough papers have referenced a particular fake reference it'll actually add that to Google Scholar and maked it look as if it's a real paper. That was a bit of an eye opener."

The "AI slop" was degrading the quality of science, Speidel said.

"The thing of course is 'will you trust me as a scientist if that stuff that I read, if that stuff's possibly made up?'"

In Australia, consulting firm Deloitte last year had to pay back $440,000 to the Australian government for a report which was found to have hallucinated references.

Deloitte later admitted it was written with the help of AI.

File photo. 123rf

Emeritus professor of engineering management at the University of York, Tony Ward, was a reviewer for one of the first academic papers to openly list AI as its lead author.

"I was quite adamant that we cannot accept that, because AI cannot be a true author, so I rejected it."

The paper was then sent back to its human authors, who tried to make the case for it being accepted.

But Ward said he declined it a second time because the review panel was not able to correspond with the author - which was required by most journals and conferences.

However, AI could be a good tool for academics, he said.

"You can use it to summarise other papers, you can get it to help in the writing process. It can do data processing and we can even use it for reviewing papers for conferences or journals."

AUT undergraduate engineering student Preston Williams agreed.

"You get stuck, you can't ask a teacher when you're studying right? You just ask AI, what is this XYZ? Half of my lecturers show me how to use AI anyway. I think you just can't get reliant off it, because then you're cooked."

World.title: New Southland wind turbines already adding power to the grid
World.content:
The head of Mercury believes powers bills will eventually benefit from more projects like the Kaiwera Downs Wind Farm.

On Wednesday, the company marked the official opening of the $600 million wind farm near Gore.

It was completed over two stages, bringing the total number of turbines to 46 and the ability to generate enough to power close to 100,000 homes.

Mercury chief executive Stew Hamilton said the turbines were already adding power to the grid.

The $486m second stage was given a green light in 2024 after Mercury signed an agreement to support Tiwai smelter - where he used to be in charge.

"I was very early, so most of that was actually being done before I moved into the chief executive role," Hamilton said.

"Obviously, I really want Tiwai to be successful, having been there previously, so super supportive of it, but largely a lot of it's handled from a commercial perspective with hands length from me."

Mercury chief executive Stew Hamilton. RNZ / Tess Brunton

Wind was cost effective and technology kept improving, and this farm was expected to last at least 30 years, he said.

"The very first wind farm that Mercury built about 30 years ago, those turbines were putting out about 600 kilowatts," he said.

"These ones are putting out nearly 4000 kilowatts. Those first turbines were about 40 metres high. These are now 156 metres high."

He believed power bills would eventually benefit from more projects like Kaiwera Downs coming online.

"The electricity component is only about 30 percent of the actual bill," Hamilton said.

"So there are other components like distribution and transmission costs. That's necessary to invest in that so New Zealand can be resilient in the long term.

"But I think as that investment comes through, we'll definitely see power prices stabilise."

While wholesale prices had come down significantly in the last six months as a result of lots of builds happening in the sector, Hamilton said that would start to flow through to residential proces over time.

Kaiwera Downs was currently the South Island's largest wind farm, although it was not expected to hold onto that title for many years.

Contact Energy has got approval for a 55-turbine wind farm on Slopedown Hill just down the road, and Mercury would soon boost turbines at Mahinerangi Wind Farm in Otago from 12 to 52.

Mercury's expansion was off the back of a power purchase option agreement with the developer of a large-scale data centre in Southland, Datagrid.

Kaiwera Downs is currently the South Island's largest wind farm. RNZ / Tess Brunton

The data centre project has faced flak from some locals who were concerned about the impact on water use, electricity prices, property values, and public health.

Hamilton acknowledged there were legitimate concerns and said he wanted to make sure those issued were covered very well.

"Really that fundamental first question that people have, where's the power going to come from? That's what we do," he said.

"We build power stations for the likes of Datagrid ... The other issues around water we've looked at very closely as well. And one of the reasons we're in the Southland is because the average temperature is less than about 10 degrees, which means that the use of water is very low."

Driving down State Highway 93, there were glimpses of turbines peeking over the hills.

But their size was not as apparent until you were next to one as it loomed 150 metres into the air.

Site manager Stuart Davie said there was a hidden network of about 90 kilometres of cables.

Site manager Stuart Davie and site health and safety officer Wayne Robson at Kaiera Downs Wind Farm. RNZ / Tess Brunton

The turbines sat in the middle of two operating farms - one with sheep and the other with cattle.

But he said the turbines did not make much noise and the stock got used to them.

"You see the cattle lying all over the pads and rubbing their backsides on the turbines and they just become part of the landscape after a while."

It was rocky terrain and he said they were blasting rock a couple of times a week for about eight months.

But the remains had been great for creating new roads - more than 30 kilometres of them - that snake through the hills.

The turbines chased the wind, often capturing the sou'wester that brought an Antarctic bite to the air, he said.

Cattle farm manager Sam Woodford said there were benefits to hosting a wind farm. RNZ / Tess Brunton

Sam Woodford managed the cattle farm that was owned by the New Zealand Super Fund.

"It was a bit of an eye-opener with the amount of machinery that come in at the start. But we work pretty well together and you look the place now, it's certainly added a lot of value," he said.

There were benefits to adding turbines to the farm.

"Going forward, it's some good income and roading maintained for the whole time as well."

Gore District Mayor Ben Bell spoke at the official opening. RNZ / Tess Brunton

The wind farm's sod-turning was Gore District Mayor Ben Bell's first official ceremony back in 2022.

"It's pretty surreal that only four years ago this was just a whole bunch of empty paddocks at the top of a hill and now there's 46 massive turbines here," he said.

It was a huge opportunity for the district, Bell said.

"Having all these projects means we can attract all sorts of different businesses from data centres to large manufacturers, really anything will need power at some stage," he said.

World.title: More women disclosing family violence to workplaces
World.content:
New research by Women's Refuge shows more women are disclosing that they are victims of family violence at work.

Under the Domestic Violence - Victim's Protection Act, introduced eight years ago, those affected by family violence are entitled to up to 10 days of paid leave a year and can request flexible working arrangements.

Women's Refuge research advisor Holly Carrington said the legislation was making a difference but there was significant room for improvement.

"There's been improvements across the board. We think the legislation raised awareness amongst employers that this is a workplace issue."

The Women's Refuge asked women who'd been victims of family violence about their experiences with their workplace.

Its report released to RNZ, Workplace Responses to Victims of Intimate Partner Violence, showed more women told their manager they were victims of family violence.

It found the numbers using paid family violence leave rose from 9 percent to almost 34 percent since the Victim's Protection Act came in to force.

The refuge collated the research from surveys done in 2019 and 2024.

Carrington said workplaces had a big role to play.

"Employment is so critical because not only it's income and potential for providing independence for that woman but also a source of social connection, self worth and self confidence...and potentially a place of safety."

Women's Refuge research advisor Holly Carrington. Supplied

More women also reported that their workplace response made them safer, this increased 20 percent to 62 percent.

"Part of it is ... keeping their information confidential. We know that oftentimes perpetrators will be really sneaky and try to get contact details of women trying to separate," Carrington said.

"It can also be just stopping someone from coming on site if the victim doesn't want them there."

Family violence expert and associate professor at the University of Auckland, Carrie Leonetti, said there were still big gaps in workplaces' responses.

Carrie Leonetti. Supplied

"That's a massive improvement but it does still mean that more than a third of women feel like the response they got from their workplace didn't make them safer," Leonetti said.

"To me the important question moving forward is what's going on in the other 38 percent of cases where they don't feel like they're being made safer."

She said family violence included financial abuse, stalking and psychological abuse.

Under the Act, workplaces could ask victims for proof of such violence.

"The statute does not indicate what on earth proof of the family violence would look like and I think this comes from a myth that people have that most family violence is physical, so people are thinking there may be medical records or there will be a police report."

Leonetti said that was concerning because a woman's disclosure of such violence should be the proof.

In her work with Shine, Mira Taitz trained people leaders and managers to respond appropriately to disclosures of family violence.

She asked employers not to ask for proof.

Shine DVFREE lead Mira Taitz. Supplied / Shine

"Most employers that we work with are really happy to overtly state in their policy that they won't be asking for proof, because that can make the difference between people coming forward to access the leave or not."

Taitz said workplaces that were clued up in their response were offering victims of family violence practical safety, such as secure carparks and blocking the perpetrator's access to the building.

"We've just seen a huge growth in awareness and normalisation that this is a workplace issue and all employers are expected and should be able to provide these entitlements safely."

The annual workplace entitlements appled to employees affected by family violence past or present.

Carrington said many women were not seeking help and this needed to change.

"The biggest barrier for women to disclose family violence is shame and embarrassment and fear of judgement," she said.

"There's a real need for employers to normalise conversations about family violence and raise awareness about it so that there's less stigma for women to come forward and seek help."
